papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.
authors: Zeyuan Ren, Guanxun Zhao, Qi Li, Hao Wang, Wenlong Liao, Keyi Luo, Xijing Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Jingye Cui, Qibin Gu, Zhichen Wang, Yucheng Hu, Liqiao Xia, Nan Bu, Zhengde Ma, Rankun Li, Xue Yang, Wende Xie

Teachers are removed at inference, preserving a standard joint-space flow-policy deployment with a learned query pathway.

Experiments on simulated and real long-horizon bimanual tasks find complementary benefits: the full model suits in-distribution settings, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
bullets: Motivates unification of vision-language-action models and world-action models despite differing architectures, outputs, and objectives.
Represents models with conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels.
Connects pretraining and offline or online post-training to policy deployment.
Instantiates the framework for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
papers.selection_reason: Unified probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models covering VLA and world-action models; directly relevant to embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
papers.tldr: A stochastic-kernel formulation unifies diverse embodied foundation models by translating their outputs into task-conditioned robot policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments. On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.
authors: Chenglong Zhang, Shuaijun Liu, Feiyang You, Shuyang Hao, Chengyu Wu, Ningxin Su
bullets: Targets coordinated multi-arm manipulation, where each arm retains local perception and action ownership.
Studies where interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how coordination should be learned.
Identifies complementary roles for shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction.
Reproduces the coordination design in a structurally different VLA architecture, suggesting backbone-agnostic applicability.

In physical experiments across four tasks, full interaction improves success over independent local policies by 16–40 percentage points; teams of three and four arms are evaluated in simulation and on hardware.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
authors: Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
bullets: Targets the repeated action-expert evaluations that make flow-matching VLAs costly for real-time robotic control.
Retains π₀.₅’s pretrained vision-language encoder and uses Mamba to model dependencies across noisy continuous-action sequences.
Compresses vision-language prefix tokens into a conditioning signal that gates and modulates Mamba blocks without repeated token-level cross-attention.
Uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment.
Improves mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three seeds, with gains also reported on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MambaAct architecture. MambaAct retains and jointly fine-tunes the pretrained π0.5 visual-language backbone while replacing its Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba-3 expert. The VLM prefix is compressed into visual, language, and learned-query global context tokens C and pooled into z, which block-specific FiLM MLPs map to scale, shift, and residual-gate parameters. The noisy action chunk Xt is projected into the initial action-token sequence H(0), while the embedded flow time ct is injected through block-specific projections. The L = 4 gated Mamba-3 blocks transform the full action-token sequence into H(L), and a final RMSNorm-linear head predicts the flow velocity V̂θ. Repeated Euler updates use this velocity to obtain the denoised action chunk X0.
Fig. 3: Real-world benchmark setups: (left) tube placing and (right) nut pouring.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot manipulation with latency reduction.
papers.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: MambaAct replaces the transformer action expert in flow-matching VLA models with a compact Mamba-based expert, substantially reducing inference latency while preserving or improving manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
bullets: Motivation: Transfer frozen VLAs such as π₀ across robot embodiments without collecting demonstrations or changing policy parameters.
Method: Train a classifier on successful source- and target-body action chunks from a few calibration tasks, then use its gradient during each denoising step to guide π₀.

Result: On LIBERO with four modified controllers, average target-body success increased from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs; 11 of 12 improved, with 5 statistically significant after Holm correction.
Scope: Guidance is data-efficient in simulation and may support sim-to-real transfer where target rollouts are costly.
Limitation: It can be ineffective or harmful for weak or locked wrists when classifier data are insufficient or favor infeasible motions; guided data and retraining can partially address this.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the transfer of frozen VLA policies (like $	extit{$ ackslash$pi$_0$}) to new robot embodiments. It uses a lightweight classifier to guide the denoising process, a transferable technique for embodied AI.
papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.tldr: A lightweight embodiment classifier can guide a frozen flow-based policy toward successful actions for a new robot body without demonstrations or policy updates, improving simulated transfer but struggling with poorly represented or infeasible dynamics.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.
authors: Victoria Smelova, Daniil Kazachkov, Georgiy Kazantsev, Iuliia Tsvetkova, Egor Cherepanov, Nikita Kachaev, Artem Latyshev, Aleksandr I. Panov, Alexey K. Kovalev
bullets: Addresses the cost and redundancy of retaining complete visual observation histories in long-horizon, multi-stage tasks.
Compares 35 plan-disagreement measures across autoregressive and flow-matching VLA policies, then validates selected signals on pretrained policies.
Uses plan-revision signals to trigger bounded visual-memory updates, with a robot-masked filter to suppress redundant frames.
Event detectors achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.981–0.997 in the reported evaluations.
The method preserved task-relevant observations until later decision points in 100% of evaluated episodes and showed transfer to real-robot replay data.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces RePlanMem-VLA, a method for selective visual memory in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. It uses replanning signals to trigger memory updates, directly addressing VLA policy limitations.
papers.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: RePlanMem-VLA uses unusually large changes in a VLA policy’s rolling action predictions to selectively store task-relevant visual keyframes.

papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
bullets: Benchmarks robustness to 11 hardware/setup perturbation axes across four LIBERO suites, with five severity levels and 210 conditions.
Evaluates nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and statistical testing.
Pooled success decreases from 0.932 under nominal conditions to 0.767 at medium severity and 0.509 at the highest severity.
Robustness varies substantially by perturbation axis and action interface.
Training on visual perturbations does not address faults that do not alter camera images; fixed-parameter episode manifests are released.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language-action robot policies under hardware perturbations, directly fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LIBERO-RIG shows that vision-language-action policies can degrade sharply under realistic robot hardware and setup changes, even when task visuals remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.
authors: Yiyang Du, Zhanqiu Guo, Haochen Zhang, Annabella Macaluso, Xin Ye, Liu Ren, Yonatan Bisk, Chenyan Xiong

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) systems already bring together two valuable resources for robot learning: rich visual representations and demonstrations of successful task execution. Intrinsic Robot Rewarding (IRR) proposes to use these resources for a second, complementary purpose: evaluating the robot's own outcomes and providing feedback for policy improvement. Successful demonstration endpoints define task-specific references, and the policy's frozen visual encoder provides the feature space in which new outcomes are assessed. The core reward mechanism adds a reference bank and a scoring operation to the existing pipeline, without requiring a separate learned evaluator or an additional perception backbone. Our position is that this reuse offers a promising route to lower integration effort, efficient reward computation, and reduced recurring human outcome scoring. Building on established research in visual rewards and learning from experience, IRR brings these ideas into the robot's existing perception and demonstration pipeline. An operational COMAU Racer 3 demonstrator is available at technology readiness level 4 (TRL 4). This laboratory foundation supports the next research step: connecting internal outcome evaluation to physical policy improvement. We present the reward formulation, central research questions, and an evaluation methodology linking reward reliability to task success and supervision effort. The intended contribution is a reusable approach to learn and improve from the data and experience already available in industrial robot systems.
bullets: Uses successful demonstration endpoints as task-specific reference outcomes.

papers.abstract: Existing adaptive reasoning methods for driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily focus on whether to reason, overlooking how reasoning should differ across driving situations. Our key insight is that while scene complexity informs reasoning depth, dynamic risk is equally critical for deciding how to reason in time-critical situations. We therefore propose CAR-VLA, a unified driving VLA model that jointly considers scene complexity and dynamic risk to guide reasoning depth, urgency, and focus. CAR-VLA maps four complexity--risk categories to three reasoning modes: \textit{Fast Intuition} for direct trajectory generation in simple low-risk scenes, \textit{Slow Thinking} for deliberate reasoning in complex low-risk scenes, and \textit{Reflex Response} for compact, hazard-focused reasoning in high-risk scenes regardless of complexity. Rather than merely shortening deliberation, Reflex Response centers reasoning on the most critical hazard and the immediate safe response. We train CAR-VLA through progressive supervised learning that links scene assessment, reasoning-mode selection, and trajectory generation, followed by reasoning-augmented reinforcement learning to improve driving quality and reasoning behavior. Experiments on NAVSIM v1(91.1 PDMS), NAVSIM v2(90.3 EPDMS), and Navhard(35.0 EPDMS) demonstrate competitive driving performance. Qualitative comparisons on navtest and in-house high-risk scenarios further illustrate risk-aware reasoning and hazard-responsive trajectory generation. The code for this paper will be released publicly at: https://github.com/chenxl124578/CAR-VLA.git
bullets: Addresses the limitation of methods that decide only whether to reason, not how reasoning should vary by situation.
Maps complexity–risk conditions to Fast Intuition, Slow Thinking, and Reflex Response modes.
Uses progressive supervised learning followed by reasoning-augmented reinforcement learning to connect scene assessment, mode selection, and trajectory generation.
Reports competitive performance on NAVSIM v1, NAVSIM v2, and Navhard, with qualitative evidence of risk-aware, hazard-responsive behavior.
Scope: high-risk situations receive compact, hazard-centered reasoning regardless of overall scene complexity.

(b) Teacher-assisted data construction produces two complementary datasets: scene assessment data containing assessment reasoning and scene labels, and mode-adaptive driving data containing scene labels, driving reasoning, and trajectories. papers.abstract: Co-training offers a straightforward way to build a multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) policy, but can fall short of the performance achieved by training each task independently. The challenge is to retain these task-specific gains in a multi-task policy without joint post-training. Combining independently trained experts through model merging is a natural approach, yet strong individual experts do not necessarily yield a strong merged policy. We identify one source of this incompatibility: task-specific changes to the action interface, comprising action normalization and the action encoder and decoder. We propose PolicyWeave, combining merge-compatible post-training with context-guided sparse merging. During post-training, all experts retain the common base policy's action interface, while task adaptation is restricted to LoRA updates in the hidden layers of the action model. This makes the experts more compatible with existing model merging methods. However, merging all experts can still introduce interference from unrelated tasks at deployment. PolicyWeave scores each expert's LoRA updates using the initial visual-language context, determines the expert set through leave-one-layer-out ranking stability, and forms a sparse weighted merge of the selected updates that remains fixed for current task. We evaluate PolicyWeave with GR00T N1.5 on 18 RoboCasa365 tasks, using only 10% of the target-task demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Preserving the shared action interface raises the average success rate across four static merging methods from 17.0% to 52.8%. PolicyWeave achieves 64.7% success with these SFT experts and 74.1% after task-specific reinforcement learning (RL), compared with 60.7% for joint RL. Further evaluations on LIBERO-10 and an AgileX Piper arm support the deployment of independently learned skills in long-horizon and real-world manipulation.
bullets: Independent task experts can outperform jointly trained policies, but incompatible action normalization and encoders/decoders make merging unreliable.
PolicyWeave keeps the base policy’s action interface fixed and restricts task adaptation to hidden-layer LoRA updates.
It scores expert updates from the initial vision-language context, selects stable experts, and creates a sparse weighted merge for each task.
On 18 RoboCasa365 tasks with 10% of target-task demonstrations, shared-interface merging increased average success from 17.0% to 52.8%; PolicyWeave reached 64.7% with SFT and 74.1% after RL.
Additional evaluations on LIBERO-10 and a real AgileX Piper arm support long-horizon and real-world manipulation use cases.

papers.abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

papers.abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. papers.abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

Text2potential creates staged potentials for dense action-chunk value-learning supervision while preserving the optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions.
Across manipulation tasks, success improves from 5.3% to 27.6%; on LIBERO-Pro, it reaches 84% under position perturbations and 76% under instruction perturbations.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We present Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) model that uses touch in two complementary ways. During pretraining, image-space contact maps derived from tactile gloves, together with features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher, supervise the visual tokens; these objectives are removed at inference. In parallel, a tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states to condition the action expert. A single checkpoint therefore supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment. To scale this supervision, we build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and pretrain Spark-0 on it together with egocentric video, robot data, and simulation. We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Spark-0 achieves the highest mean success rate on both SparkArena tracks and ranks first on all eight aggregate metrics of the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark. Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining. The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.
authors: Tianxing Chen, Wenwei Lin, Chuqiao Lyu, Peicheng Xiang, Junyuan Tang, Tian Nian, Zijian Cai, Kehe Ye, Chenze Yu, Wenxuan Zhu, Eric J. Chen, Yan Qin, Yue Chen, Tongyu Wu, Junhao Gong, Kai-Chong Lei, Jiahao Zhang, Kailun Su, Qiwei Liang, Renjing Xu, Ping Luo, Wenbo Ding
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sensing force, compliance, and incipient slip from images alone.
Pretrains a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action model using tactile contact maps and frozen 3D geometry features to supervise visual tokens.
Adds a tactile pathway encoding regional force histories and 3D taxel states for action conditioning, while supporting vision-only deployment from one checkpoint.
Introduces HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour human tactile manipulation dataset, and SparkArena for unified simulated and real-robot evaluation.

Reports improved performance: vision-only Ego Humanoid success rises from 52.5% to 71.7%, while tactile-conditioned SparkArena-Real success rises from 44.0% to 52.0% when touch is retained during pretraining.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle
bullets: Pretrained exclusively on curated public robot, egocentric human, and vision-language data.
Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.
Outperformed only by roughly twice-as-large models on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand, and RoboCasa365.

Figure 3: REKI. (a) Camera views and instruction are encoded as context Et, which every expert block reads by cross-attention. The state embedding gt and the flow time modulate the actions through adaptive normalisation. The noisy chunk enters the expert’s stream, and the flow loss compares the predicted velocity with its target. The register keys and values of past frames are kept in a cache and read by self-attention, which is the memory of §4.1. (b) One of the ten blocks, holding nr=32 registers and the action tokens of the current frame. Arrows run from a query to what it reads. Action tokens read the current and past registers and themselves, and registers never read them.

Figure 2: How VLAs carry the past. Each panel shows one training window of three frames, with a loss under each frame that receives one. (a) Past frames enter the VLM with the current one, in full (Yuan et al., 2026), compressed (Torne et al., 2026; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) or from a cache (Jang et al., 2025). The VLM takes the whole window as input, and only the last frame is supervised. (b) A state is written at each step and read at the next, in the backbone (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) or as fast weights in the head (Jiang et al., 2026). Each step needs the output of the previous one, so the window is unrolled step by step. (c) Each frame is encoded on its own, and an added module mixes the memory tokens of past frames into the prediction for the current one. HAMLET (Koo et al., 2026) supervises the last frame only, and MemoryVLA (Shi et al., 2026) every frame, with the bank entries stored without gradient. (d) In REKI, the memory tokens are registers in the action expert. Their keys and values are kept across frames and read by the self-attention already present. The window is one batched pass, and every frame receives a loss.

(b) The registers and noisy action tokens of a frame cross-attend the context of that frame and self-attend the registers of the K frames up to it, so the past reaches the current chunk only through the registers, and only these are kept for later frames.

(c) Two-arm tasks move both arms in at least 80% of the successful episodes with memory, one-arm tasks a single arm. The three other tasks are left out. (d) On one H100. The numbers give the difference to K=1 in ms.

Right: task score of REKI with and without memory and of π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) on two shorter- and three longer-horizon tasks, over 10 episodes each. Solid bars give full successes, hatched bars partial credit.

Figure 10: Register cache at inference (K=3). (a) In the first Euler step of a chunk, the VLM encodes the current frame t. The registers of frame t read its context and the cached registers of frames t−1 and t−2. The action tokens read the context and the registers of the three frames; past frames are not encoded again. (b) In the N−1 other Euler steps, only the action tokens are updated, and they read the context and the register keys and values from the cache. The registers do not read the action tokens and skip adaptive normalisation, so they do not depend on the flow time and are computed once per frame. When the next frame enters, the registers of frame t−2 are dropped.

Frames are one chunk apart (1 s), and A and B mark the two poses the arm alternates between. In the top row, the two arms swap at every chunk, one reaching while the other retracts. In the bottom row, a single arm moves back and forth. The blocks do not move in either row.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets VLA inference bottlenecks caused by hundreds of visual tokens from high-resolution, multi-view observations.
Ranks tokens using task-to-vision attention rather than generic visual saliency.
Adapts compression rates from attention-distribution uniformity using an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
Evaluated across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT in LIBERO, SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Reduces simulation backbone FLOPs by 35–59% and action latency by 9–32% while maintaining success; real-robot end-to-end latency drops 20% at comparable success.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of FastVLA, our temporally adaptive, training-free visual token compression framework for Vision-Language-Action models. At each action prediction step, FastVLA estimates task-conditioned patch importance via attention, measures distributional uniformity over selected vision tokens, and dynamically adjusts the compression rate using an online sliding-window calibration. By retaining task-relevant yet information-diverse tokens across timesteps, our approach reduces LLM backbone computation while preserving action performance.

We further provide complete rollout videos with pruning effect by FastVLA in the supplementary material.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.

(2) Context encoding compresses visual tokens Vt−1 and timestamp tokens Tt−1 into a compact representation qt−1 using a learnable query Q. (3) Hidden state updates mt that captures local dynamics and st that preserves global semantics. (4) LoRA weights are decoded from the hidden states. (5) st is updated through gated summation.

Figure 3 Overview of the MaLoW data pipeline and statistics of MaLoW-Instruct. (1): Our data pipeline consists of a Question Generator, an Answer Generator, and a Verifier. (2): The distribution of the streaming question timing, the question type, and video source in MaLoW-Instruct.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overall pipeline. (a) Two-Axis Trigger. The VLA policy generates two initial action chunk samples, based on which the two-axis trigger decides whether to activate repeated sampling. (b) Latent World Model Verifier. If triggered, the verifier evaluates K candidate chunks and selects the one with the highest estimated delta progress for execution. The JEPA-based latent world model autoregressively takes states, actions, and observations as input and predicts delta progress in the latent space. (c) Attention Mask. The delta progress key is designed to be invisible from other queries to remove possible task-specific shortcuts for world modeling.
Figure 7. Critical Index and Critical Moments in LIBERO.
Figure 8. Critical Index and Critical Moments in RoboTwin.

Figure 2. Conceptual comparison between different paradigms. (a1) Sampling-and-selection with VLM: Directly predict the delta progress with the current observation and the action chunk produced by VLAs. (a2) Sampling-and-selection with generative models: Extract the delta progress after generating the estimated future. papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.
authors: Haitao Shen, Hanyu Liu, Yihan Lin, Huiping Liu, Junbo Cui, Daoheng Li, Yang Li, Jing Zhang, Wenxin Li, Yuan Yao

papers.abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
authors: Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang

papers.abstract: While generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open-world manipulation, real-world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like "make me a sandwich" requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures. To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user-level and scene-level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control-based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference-consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety-finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Baekseung Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Existing adaptive execution methods rely on generation stability or prediction agreement, which may not reflect task-completion potential.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of repeatedly recomputing task context in VLA policies.
Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.
A lightweight actor combines current visual/proprioceptive feedback with learned time- and arm-indexed queries to predict action chunks.
Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $\pi_{0.5}$ as LTM-$\pi$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$\pi$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
authors: Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang
bullets: Stores consecutive-observation transitions in latent form rather than retaining full visual history.
Combines a frozen latent action encoder, lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental, annotation-free inference.
LTM-π reaches 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem without external reasoning models or memory annotations.
Memory scales effectively: RoboMME success rises to 87.50% with tenfold more demonstrations and remains 84.00% under a 200-token budget.
Real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%; a Cup Swap diagnostic underscores the importance of process supervision for temporal composition.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
authors: Qi Lu, Jiarun Li, Ce Zhang, Miao Pan, Yi Pan, Xu Wang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Most VLA models learn observation-to-action mappings without direct supervision of intermediate physical changes, risking overfitting.
The framework uses current-to-future physical state changes as explicit targets, including task-relevant semantics and visual motion.
A large-scale pretraining dataset provides annotations for these state transitions.
At inference, actions are generated directly from current observations without extra inference overhead.
It is competitive on LIBERO and RoboTwin and outperforms π₀.₅ in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Spatial augmented reality (SAR) augments physical environments with projected content, but most systems assume that the projector pose, target region, or motion path has been fixed or specified. We instead make projected light an embodied action: given a language instruction and current visual observations, a system must decide how to move and where and at what scale to place the projection. We introduce LICOA to realize this capability. Its differential-drive chassis provides room-scale approach and repositioning, while a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF) and projection scale provide rapid local control of the beam. A shared interface maps synchronized external and onboard RGB cameras with robot control state to physical optical actions across pretrained action models. Because instruction-conditioned optical action lacks dedicated training data and a common evaluation protocol, we construct a matched simulation embodiment and a corpus with 150 tasks and 7,500 rendered episodes, then evaluate models trained only on this corpus in previously unseen real-world environments. Across 480 complete closed-loop real-world execution trials (rollouts) on 12 tasks, the best adapted action model achieves a 57.50% success rate and 40.64% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33% and 5.15% for the same architecture trained from scratch. A further 150 real-world ablation rollouts support the need for both camera views and coordinated control of the chassis and mirror. These results establish a physical platform, shared perception and optical action interface, corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol for treating projected light as an embodied action.
authors: Yuchen Deng, Shunkai Zhou, Ruixuan Zhu, Haibin Ling, Bingyao Huang
bullets: Addresses SAR settings where projector pose, target region, and motion path are not fixed in advance.
Combines differential-drive chassis movement with 2DoF steerable-mirror and projection-scale control.
Introduces a shared interface linking synchronized external/onboard RGB observations and robot state to optical actions.
Provides a simulation embodiment, 150-task/7,500-episode corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol.
In 480 real-world trials, the best adapted model achieved 57.50% success and 40.64% success weighted by path length; ablations support using both camera views and coordinated chassis–mirror control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

bullets: Prior VLA research mainly evaluates What-level instructions that specify the task, overlooking How-level instructions that specify execution.

SIMPLER-IN evaluates instruction-specific success beyond standard benchmarks and reveals poor generalization to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions.
How-level instruction following remains an open challenge.

papers.abstract: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
authors: Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in proactive assistance, where identical behaviors may indicate different user needs.
Uses a VLM task predictor with Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) to select when and how to assist, and a VLA executor to perform tasks.
Represents routines as a finite-state machine with activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions.
A reflection VLM updates PAM from daily interaction traces without weight updates or retraining.
In a 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, the system improved with experience, achieved the best reported precision, recall, and F1, and reduced first-fire delay from about 5 seconds to 1 second.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. (a) A VLM task predictor reads PAM and recent frames to select assistive tasks for the VLA executor. (b) At the end of each day, a VLM memory reflector updates PAM from the day’s video by adding or revising states, trigger-action pairs, and transitions.

Figure 5: Multi-day proactive task prediction (Days 1–5). Memory-free baselines show limited T1–T6 recall overall, while Ours (FSM Memory) consistently improves across days, achieving the highest F1 and reducing first-fire delay from ∼5 s on Day 1 to ∼1 s by Day 5.

papers.abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
bullets: Unifies fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated triggers as special cases of Value of Intervention; periodic scheduling is optimal when collapse is state-independent.
Adaptive scheduling benefits depend on intervention cost relative to fast-policy operation and on heterogeneity in policy collapse.
At intermediate cost (ρ=1.53), the adaptive trigger follows its predicted threshold, but language rewrites fail to improve either LIBERO suite; only reverting failed rewrites avoids net downside.
A leak-free evaluation protocol reduces apparent early-warning AUC from 0.93 to 0.62 across 929 deployment traces.
A detection-limited theorem and compilation loop connect measured intervention value to schedulability and produce refresh periods within 2.4% of a closed-loop oracle.

(c) The standard: a four-measure leak-free protocol and a distillation loop that compiles the measured staleness value function into per-task refresh periods.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies requires costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and controller-compatible whole-body state-action labels. Egocentric human demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA (Kinematics-Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific whole-body state-action supervision. KODA first generates a simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this canonical record and regenerates whole-body state-action supervision for co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets, suggesting potential for further scaling.
authors: Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Junsong Wu, Weiji Xie, Qingyao Xu, Sheng Yin, Shiqing Wang, Jiyuan Shi, Siheng Chen, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the costly need for robot demonstrations with aligned observations and whole-body state-action labels.
Generates a simulator-checked canonical whole-body trajectory from sparse human motion using sampling-based command optimization.
Uses the trajectory to synthesize aligned robot-camera observations, then regenerates controller-specific actions and proprioceptive states.
Evaluated on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks with SONIC and HEFT controllers.
With fixed robot data, success on human-covered but robot-unseen conditions improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points; performance trends upward with more human data.

The resulting data are combined with matching real-robot demonstrations to co-train a controller-specific vision–language–action (VLA) policy for language-guided humanoid loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Apoorva Vashisth, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses limitations of 2D, task-agnostic, and manually annotated task-specific grasping methods.
Uses vision-language reasoning to infer semantic affordances from the task and object geometry.
Refines the task-informed grasp prior with 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency.
Reports a 94% success rate on TaskGrasp, compared with 74% for the best baseline.
Demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world objects on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of TGrasp6D. Given a single RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction, a vision-language model identifies and localizes the task-relevant affordance and predicts an image-space grasp orientation. These cues are lifted into 3D to form a task-informed grasp prior, from which candidate 6DoF grasps are sampled and refined for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency, yielding the final task-oriented grasp.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of different 6DoF TOG approaches on objects from the TaskGrasp [9] dataset. For each method, we show 5 task-oriented grasps per object. Compared to other approaches, our TGrasp6D produces more successful grasps across diverse object types and tasks. For cases like “scoop[ing]” with the “spoon,” most approaches generate feasible grasps. However, performance drops sharply for more challenging cases like doing a “handover” with the “measuring cup.” Of note, compared to the pure vision-language prior (f), grasp-pose refinement (g) appears to visually diversify grasps by generating feasible stable and task-consistent alternates. In some cases, like the “measuring cup,” it even recovers some failures despite noise and missing points due to occlusion in the object point-cloud.

Fig. 1: Example of TGrasp6D producing distinct 6DoF grasps for different tasks on the same real-world object. “handover” task results in grasps that keep the handle clear whereas tasks like “pound” and “cook” that require holding the hammer and pan from the handle are reflected.

Fig. 4: Analysis of failure modes, including the effect of grasp refinement for GPT-5.5. Note the y-axis breaks between 4%-10% and 12%-19% to accommodate Gemini-3.7 (11.0%) and Qwen3.5-35B (19.7%) without compressing the smaller values.

TABLE I: Comparison with baseline methods. Note that fOE and fPE are reported only for grasps marked as failures. All baseline results use unmodified author-released code and, where available, author-provided pretrained weights; we do not alter any baseline’s inference pipeline.
TABLE II: Real-robot task-oriented grasping success rate comparison.
