papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
authors: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi, Usha Bhalla, Thomas Icard, Matt Feiszli, Thomas McGrath, Vasudev Shyam, Demba Ba, Leon Bergen, Nina Miolane, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel

Finds geometries are predominantly multi-dimensional and reflect the constraints under which the robot acts.

Top: held-out decoded directions (VLM layer 21), averaged in 6 cm cells in a target-centered frame; arrow length is cell coherence. Bottom left: as in Fig. 3c, but for direction probes fit on different halves of the houses: the near/far cosine stays below its ceiling at every boundary (0.081 vs. 0.130 at c = 15). Bottom right: the range-split pair does not outperform a single recalibrated probe on near reads (up to 3◦ worse) and improves on it by at most 1.1◦ on far reads — a single probe suffices at all ranges.

Figure 22: After a full turn of the wrist joint the action expert’s activation does not return to its start; the VLM’s returns exactly. From one pose of the roll sweep (App. C.8; a single house), the wrist joint (Franka joint 7) is driven through successive full turns by writing the joint value directly into the simulator, far past the joint’s physical range (shaded band), so the sweep tests the models’ inputs rather than a reachable motion. At every full turn (dashed lines, large markers) the rendered frames and text tokens are identical to the start and only the raw joint value differs, and only the action expert receives that value. (Left) Action expert, layer 9, first action token: Euclidean distance of the activation at each step from the start activation; after one turn it is 28.8 units away and does not return over the following turns. (Right) VLM, layer 20, mean over image tokens: the same distance, which varies within each turn and is exactly 0 at every full turn; the two panels are in different activation units.

Figure 3: MolmoBot’s VLM encodes distance to the target in nearly orthogonal near- and far-range codes (layer 21). (a) Near (<15 cm) and far (15–70 cm) probe R2 after erasing the top-k directions of the other probe, computed against each range’s own variance. Erasing far directions leaves near decoding intact while far decoding collapses, and vice versa. The intact (k = 0) probes have errors of ∼1.3 cm (near) and ∼3.6 cm (far). (b) Near R2 (<c) vs. far R2 (≥c) as the cutoff c is swept. Clipped (‘round to c’) probes match probes fit separately on each range and outperform a single full-range probe. (c) Cosine between the near- and far-probe weight vectors as the cutoff c is swept, for range-split and clipped (‘round to c’) pairs (fold mean ± s.d.). For c ≲ 30 cm, both cosines stay below the cosine between two copies of the same probe fit on different halves of the data (dashed). On synthetic activations that encode distance along a single direction, the same probes are nearly parallel for c ≳ 15 cm (dotted). (d) Activations plotted by their meter- and centimeter-probe readouts, colored by true distance in meters (left) and centimeters (right). Far samples vary along the meter axis while the centimeter readout saturates, and near samples do the opposite, tracing an L.

Figure 9: The action expert (layer 12) also maintains a rank-3 EE position subspace. Panels as in the top and middle rows of Figure 2, for EE position read from the action expert, which receives proprioception; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The readout is near-exact and the paths are recovered almost without distortion. The gap between the general-linear and orthogonal residuals shows the subspace is a scaled, not isometric, copy of world coordinates.

Figure 10: The action expert (layer 22) also maintains a rank-3 target object position subspace. Panels as in Figure 9, for the target object’s position; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The action expert receives the object only through cross-attention to the VLM, and it carries target position with larger error than the VLM (Figure 2), recovering the paths with more distortion.

Figure 11: Within a scene, target object position is computed on the VLM’s instruction and final tokens between layers 12 and 21 and appears in the action expert from layer 18; EE position is present from the first layer in both. Held-out R2 of the rank-3 ridge readout of end-effector position (left) and target object position (right) at every layer, scored after removing each held-out house’s mean from the true and predicted positions, so only position changes within a scene count; one line per VLM token pool, the action expert dashed, rings on the readouts of Figure 2, values below the axis floor clipped. The target’s height is constant within a scene, so the target panel’s variance is horizontal and any within-scene variation in the predicted height counts as error; scores fall below zero where a readout’s predictions vary within a scene without tracking the object. On the instruction and final tokens the target read stays at or below zero until layer 12 and peaks at layers 18–21, while the image patches carry little of it at any layer. The action expert tracks EE position near-perfectly at every layer and the target only from layer 18 on.

Figure 12: Distance is compressive within the near range and closest to linear beyond 30 cm, and each ruler reads only its own range (VLM, layer 21). (Left) Held-out mean absolute error per bin of true distance for a single full-range ridge probe fit to d, log d, or 1/d and mapped back to metres; the compressive links have the lower error below 15 cm and the linear link in the farthest bins. (Right) Held-out R2 against true distance for the centimeter ruler and the meter ruler of Figure 3, scored separately on states below and above that cutoff; negative (saturated) values are drawn at zero and printed. Each ruler saturates outside its own range, as does a single unclipped metre-scale probe (not shown) on the near-range states.

Figure 29: DROID real world behavioral manifolds. Here we show the behavioral manifolds realized by MolmoAct2 and π0.5. The EE position and wrist orientation point clouds show the activations of all 3,321 queries, sampled from MolmoAct2 AE L16 of 36 and π0.5 VLM L7 of 18, demonstrating the structures appear across multiple streams. We plot a natural episode trajectory in the EE position subplots and the wrist roll sweep of Figure 30 in the Wrist Orientation subplots. In the Gripper plot we project the 379 landmark activations from each model’s final action-expert block onto the principal components of the pullback steering vectors, with binned steering vectors as arrows.

Figure 26: Gripper control for action expert layer 9 (Top left) A linear probe decodes the commanded gripper aperture; one principal component of the pullback steering vectors decodes it nearly as well as the full activation. (Top right) Natural-rollout activations colored by gripper state; notably, the steering vectors from each cluster do not point toward the other, unlike layer 32 in Figure 7. (Bottom left) One component captures ∼55% of steering-vector variance. (Bottom right) One component flips the gripper but leaks into the arm joints relative to using the full 768-dimensional steering vector; more components remove this excess leakage.

Figure 16: Contact is decodable from the wrist-camera patches at the first layer and from the exo-camera patches and text tokens at a similar level only from the middle layers on (VLM). (Left) Held-out AUC of the contact discriminant at each of 10 layers, fit separately on five token groups: wrist-camera patches, exo-camera patches, text tokens, the final token, and the whole-sequence mean; reference lines mark a phase-timer baseline, a gripper-closure baseline, and the action expert. (Right) Per-patch AUC at layer 24 for the two cameras: the signal is spread over the whole image rather than confined to the fingers.

Figure 18: Under the frozen read, the decoded phase shifts toward grasp in all three streams, while place landmarks are most often still decoded as place. Left to right: action expert, VLM vision tokens, VLM language tokens. Each row gives the percentage of one phase’s landmarks decoded as each phase when the policy is shown the current frame twice (bold: the true phase); the strip beneath each matrix gives the percentage decoded correctly with the usual two frames, at the same moments.

Figure 19: Per-step time course of the freezing effect on gripper commands. Fraction of chunks commanding a closed gripper at each step of the executed action chunk (shaded: 95% CI), natural vs. frozen, per phase.

Figure 23: Even the most circular reachable wrist rotation does not close. Instead of rolling about the gripper’s approach axis, we tilt the gripper 30◦ off that axis and orbit the tilt about the vertical. If driven through a full turn, this precession returns the wrist orientation exactly to its start (a closed circle in SO(3)). The gripper position is held fixed within 5 cm while the whole arm reconfigures, and we record activations at each step. The arm’s joint limits (clipped to the 1st to 99th training percentile) stop the orbit partway: sweeping both directions from the start covers −70◦ to +158◦ (228◦ of the turn; angles are the realized rotation about the vertical axis). (Top) PCA over the sweep activations. Precession remains an open arc, with PC1 carrying 69% of the variance and PC2 25%. (Bottom) The exo camera image at different rotation angles along the sweep.

Figure 35: Arm and object placements in the crossed teleport harvest used for EE and target position. Robot-base frame viewed from above (left) and from the side, with height above the object’s resting position (right). Gray points are arm poses and violet diamonds object placements across all houses; the dashed outline is the box arm poses are sampled in. For one example house, the black point is the home pose, blue points its ten arm poses, and violet diamonds its five object placements; unlike Figure 15, both the arm and the object move.

Figure 21: The VLM maintains only a weak, pixel-derived trace of wrist orientation. A roll sweep from the same starting pose as Figure 6, over a 332◦ range (−156◦ to +176◦), read at the VLM; the VLM receives only images and text as input. (Left) PCA over the sweep activations (layer 35). The trace wraps — −156◦ and +176◦ land close together — but does not form a clean circle. (Right) The reduced-rank regression of Figure 24 at every VLM layer, on natural rollouts re-encoded at the VLM (19,089 states, 169 houses). Decoding peaks mid-stack at R2 = 0.31 (layer 20), a third of the action expert’s 0.87 (dotted) on the same data.

Figure 27: In the VLM backbone, gripper steerability falls to the control floor by layer 28 although aperture readability stays high. The gripper pullback of App. C.9 with the edit δ added to every sequence token after VLM block L, at screen scale (32 edits per layer and objective, one query per landmark). (Left) Fraction of edits that flip the commanded gripper under the arm-hold objective of App. C.9 and under the gripper-only objective (the arm-hold and smoothness terms dropped), counted on the 29 edits whose unedited chunk has the opposite gripper sign; the gray band spans the flip rates of a control edit (the mean of the action-expert catalog, App. C.9). (Middle) Held-out R2 of a ridge probe from the pre-edit activation to the commanded aperture, best of the token pools at each layer; readability rises to 0.86 by layer 20. (Right) Absolute cosine between the first principal component of the arm-hold edits, a sample-limited estimate from the small per-layer catalog, and the close–open flip axis (dashed: the action-expert catalog of Figure 26); at the shallowest flipping layers (4 and 12) the leading component is only partly aligned with the flip axis.

Figure 28: The gripper steering vectors stay dominated by one component and aligned with the flip axis at every action-expert layer. The pullback catalog of App. C.9, re-fit at layers 9, 18, 27, and 32. (Left) Share of steering-vector variance on the first principal component. (Middle) Stable rank of the steering vectors. (Right) Cosine between the first principal component and the flip axis (mean close edit minus mean open edit), and held-out R2 of the aperture probe restricted to that component; dashed: a random direction.

Figure 36: The VLM keeps the target’s position but no map of the workspace; other objects are encoded per image patch. (Left) A table-occupancy map of the target, read from VLM activations (last token, layer 21), is no more accurate than the same readout applied to the target’s three true coordinates (dashed). (Middle) One readout shared across all image-patch tokens detects whether an object the instruction does not name is visible in that patch, well above patch-position and patch-color baselines (exo and wrist cameras, layers 8 and 20). (Right) With scene means removed, a readout of table position fit on all visible objects does not track the target as it moves, whereas one fit on the instructed target alone does on the exo camera.

Figure 31: MolmoAct2 and π0.5 encode distance to target object in 2 orthogonal subspaces. We find that similar to MolmoBot, as shown in Fig. 3 the tested DROID model also encode distance to target object with a multi-scale ruler. We sample 26,675 timesteps from 1,998 pick and place episodes. The distance is how far the gripper is from its initial grasp location. Activations are sampled from MolmoAct2 VLM L25 of 36 and π0.5 VLM L14 of 18.

Figure 24: Full 3-DOF wrist orientation is decodable from natural rollouts at low rank (AE). Unlike Fig. 6, which rotates a single roll joint and reads the code with PCA, here “wrist orientation” means the complete 3-DOF orientation of the hand, represented by the first two columns of its rotation matrix (a 6-D target). We fit reduced-rank ridge regressions of rank 1 to 6 from the activations to this target on natural rollouts (6,555 queries, 191 houses) and report R2 on held-out houses at six action-expert layers. Rank 2 recovers most of the decodable variance and rank 3 nearly all of it; higher ranks add little. Decodability peaks at layer 9.

Figure 32: Task phase subspace in π0.5 and MolmoAct2. (Left) Example trajectory for a simple pick-and-place task, “Pick up the white and green brush from the table and hang it on the wall,” along with the predicted task phases. The ground-truth bar is derived from the measured gripper aperture alone, using a simple heuristic: reach until the gripper starts to close, grasp while it closes, transport while it stays closed, place after it opens. A linear classifier is trained on the top 48 principal components of activations collected across 2,000 episodes. (Right) The recovered task subspace in both models, colored by phase. Activations are taken from the π0.5 action expert at layer 9 of 18 and the MolmoAct2 action expert at layer 22 of 36.

Figure 4: MolmoBot’s VLM encodes contact with the target along a direction that survives off-schedule contact (layer 24). (a) Natural rollouts projected onto their first three principal components, colored by contact; the two states separate cleanly. (b) An LDA probe trained on natural rollouts decodes contact with 91.3% accuracy. When we force an early touch or an induced slip by teleporting the object, the same probe still decodes contact well above chance.

Figure 6: The action expert encodes wrist orientation as an open arc, and edits to it act as beliefs (layer 9). We sweep the wrist’s roll joint through its full range (−172.8◦ to +172.8◦), holding other joints fixed, and record activations at each angle (camera views in Fig. 20). (a) The sweep traces an open curve: its endpoints, nearly the same physical pose, lie far apart. (b) An autoencoder maps activations onto an exact circle. (c) A single ±20◦ or ±40◦ edit produces a decoded rotation opposing the written angle (dots: seven held-out scenes; ticks: means; dashed diagonal: the response a command would produce). (d) Holding the edit at every step compounds the corrections, rotating the wrist opposite the written angle by about its magnitude (vertical lines mark action chunks).

Figure 7: Gripper control is one-dimensional (AE, layer 32). (a) The first principal component of the pullback steering vectors captures ∼70% of their variance. (b) One principal component of the pullback steering vectors decodes the commanded gripper aperture nearly as well as the full activation. (c) Natural-rollout activations colored by gripper state; the steering vectors point from each cluster toward the other. (d) One component flips the gripper but leaks into the arm joints relative to using the full 768-dimensional steering vector; more components remove this excess leakage.

Figure 13: The action expert (layer 35) reproduces the two-subspace distance code. Same store, folds, and constructions as Figure 3, read from the action expert instead of the VLM. (Top left) Held-out R2 of the near and far decodes as far-axis (solid) or near-axis (dashed) directions are erased; each decode drops only when its own axis is removed. (Top right) Held-out R2 of the centimeter and meter rulers on each side of the 15 cm cutoff; each ruler scores only its own range, and bars below zero are drawn at zero with the value printed. (Bottom) The two ruler readouts plotted against each other, colored by true distance on the meter (left) and centimeter (right) scales; the meter ruler resolves the far arm and the centimeter ruler the near arm, as in the VLM cell.

Figure 15: Object teleportation across the workspace for distance to target object experiments. Object placements in the robot-base frame, viewed from above (robot at left, forward to the right). Gray points are all placements in the teleport datasets (906 houses). For one example house, the black point is the object’s natural placement and the blue points its 15 teleported placements, sampled uniformly over the supporting surface within the benchmark placement envelope; dashed arrows connect the natural placement to each teleport. Only the object is moved; the arm’s initial pose is unchanged.

Figure 17: MolmoBot’s task phase subspace in the VLM backbone (vision tokens, Layer 31). (Left) LDA projection of natural rollouts, colored by phase (0.86 balanced accuracy across held-out houses; AE: 0.92). (Middle) The full three-dimensional LDA subspace, with a held-out episode’s trajectory traversing the four phase regions in order. (Right) Freezing shifts the VLM’s decoded phase toward grasp, as in the action expert (Figure 5): frozen reach and grasp landmarks are mostly decoded as grasp, and frozen transport and place landmarks are most often still decoded as transport and place.

Figure 30: Wrist orientation PCA across models and streams. Following Fig. 6, we record a real-robot episode in which the wrist roll joint is swept from −79◦ to +84◦ while the other joints and the scene are held approximately fixed, and plot the top two principal components of the activations for MolmoAct2 and π0.5 in both the VLM and the action expert (color: roll angle). As in MolmoBot, the sweep traces an open, semicircular arc. Because real-world data are noisier, the trajectories are considerably less smooth.

Figure 25: Cumulative variance of gripper steering vectors in layer 32. Cumulative explained variance from PCA on the pullback steering vectors δ (App. C.9) as a function of the number of principal components. The first component captures ∼70% of the variance, complementing the per-component view in Figure 7.

Figure 20: Wrist roll sweep (Figure 6). Exo (third-person) camera images at several points of the sweep through the wrist’s full roll range (−172.8◦ to +172.8◦), with all other joints fixed. Borders are colored by wrist angle θ.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representational geometry in vision-language-action policies for robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA policies encode task-relevant concepts as structured, often multi-dimensional geometries shaped by physical and task constraints—not merely as linearly readable variables.

papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin, Dron Hazra, Usha Bhalla, Curt Tigges, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Recover task-relevant features spanning perception, language, proprioception, episode phase, and control variables.
Causal interventions show that steering visual, semantic, and spatial features predictably changes action predictions.
Feature-based data attribution traces failure-recovery behavior to fewer than 1.4% of training tokens.
Results support matching featurizers to representation geometry for more effective robot behavior analysis and modification.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates block-sparse featurizers in VLA models, with causal steering and feature-based data attribution for robot behavior.
papers.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Block-sparse featurizers expose interpretable, multidimensional features in robot foundation models, enabling precise behavior steering and targeted training-data shaping.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay, Eric Bigelow, Andrew Lee, Conor Watts, Thomas Icard, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Studies how perceptual and semantic representations become actions in three frontier VLA models: π₀.₅, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot.
Activation patching identifies mid-to-late cross-attention layers as the main causal pathway into the action expert.
Early-to-mid representations of target nouns determine object selection, while later text representations encode spatial redirection.
Spatial information is stored differently across architectures, including instruction-following text positions and image-token positions.
Restricting MolmoBot conditioning to 3 of 36 layers cuts inference FLOPs by up to 33% while retaining comparable success; the approach also transfers to real-robot π₀.₅ deployment.

(Left) We copy activations from a donor episode (“Pick up the banana”) into a target episode (“Pick up the apple”) with the position of the objects swapped. Visual information (purple) sits in early image tokens, semantic information (blue) in the early noun token, and geometric information (orange) in later text tokens. The action expert (AE) reads from a narrow band of later layer. (Top right) Schematic of these effects by layer. The action expert reads from a narrow band of layers.(Bottom right) Keeping only this interface in MolmoBot, 3 of 36 connections, cuts compute by 33% with comparable average success (46.7% vs. 46.9%) over 3000 trials.

Curves show normalized trajectory shift E toward the reference trajectory (same scene other object requested) after patching one action-expert connection (left) or three consecutive connections (right, indexed by the center layer). The results shown are computed across 144,768 patches over 26 scenes via averaging comparisons B and C (Section 4.1).

Figure 4: Backbone interventions trace the construction of the geometric variable in MolmoAct2 and π0.5. Colors show normalized trajectory shift E toward the other-object trajectory in the original scene. Each cell averages 416 interventions: 26 original–counterfactual pairs, each tested in both directions under eight noise seeds. The visual, semantic, and geometric hypotheses predict the signatures in Figure 3a. We omit MolmoAct2 layers 27–35 as they have |E| < 0.001.

(a) The input changes in A, B and C produce distinct causal signatures for each interchange intervention type. (b) Green arrows show the unpatched behavior; red arrows show predicted recipient behavior if the patch transfers the labeled information. These labels denote transfer hypotheses, not information uniquely isolated by single comparisons. For example, in A, patching scene-layout information through an image patch can produce the same behavioral shift as patching target-object identity through a noun patch. We therefore interpret effects jointly across the comparisons and patched token positions.

Figure 6: MolmoBot backbone patching across 13 object pairs. Same comparisons, token groups, and metric as Figure 4. Each cell averages 416 patches: 26 donor–recipient pairs, each patched in both directions under eight noise seeds. Figure 8: Counterfactual scenes. Object pairs used each shown in both layouts with the objects’ left–right positions exchanged. Images show the exterior DROID camera, cropped to the table (during experiments the full frame is used).

Figure 5: Complementary and full-trajectory interface patching. (a) Normalized trajectory shift E when patching all connections except one (left) or except three consecutive connections (right). Horizontal axes index the unchanged connection or window center. (b) RMS displacement in millimeters after patching only a single connection (left) or three consecutive connections (right, indexed by their center). papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic causal analysis of vision-language-action robot models with efficiency gains, directly fitting embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
papers.tldr: Causal analysis reveals a narrow action-conditioning interface in VLA models, enabling substantial inference savings with comparable manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.
bullets: A LoRA-adapted WAM generates plausible video but systematically mis-targeted actions on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
The method estimates hand poses from generated video, converts them to actions with inverse kinematics, and uses them as preferred fine-tuning targets.
A hybrid DPO+SFT+DTW objective performs best, outperforming supervised relabeling and plain Flow-DPO.
Recovered-action gating raises pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success from approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% to 75%, 47%, and 42%.
On the reported objects, the best model achieves 90% pre-grasp/20% full-task success on Oreo and 80%/30% on a held-out object.

papers.selection_reason: Adapts a world-action model to a new robot via cross-modal self-distillation from generated video to actions; directly relevant to robot learning and VLA.
papers.title: AutodidactWAM: Cross-Modal Self-Distillation from Generated Video to Robot Actions

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023
bullets: Compliance is essential for contact-rich tasks but is not captured by common robot demonstration interfaces.
Four-channel bilateral teleoperation uses the leader arm to measure intended equilibrium separately from realized pose and force.
Per-axis, direction-dependent stiffness is recovered by regression without dedicated force/tactile hardware or manual annotation.
The resulting labels fine-tune a VLA to output stiffness alongside pose.
In a Franka Research 3 wiping task, commanded contact force rose from 6.4 N for normal wiping to 9.1 N for firm wiping; the policy was the only one of five to respond this way.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
authors: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness.

Uses navigation-conditioned world-model rollouts that simulate strictly following instructions to assess their safety.
Achieves 88.16 Driving Score and 68.64% Success Rate on Bench2Drive.
Improves closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 versus the best SimLingo variant.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.

papers.abstract: Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken. After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks. The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.
bullets: Addresses robots’ tendency to wait for complete instructions before acting.
Uses a fine-tuned text encoder to score scene objects word by word and commits when the best calibrated probability reaches a user-set threshold.
Supports waiting or asking when confidence is insufficient, with 1 − τ representing accepted error risk.
On instructions with unseen words, it commits correctly 1.6–2× as often as keyword matching and is at least 92% correct at τ = 0.9.
Runs in 31–35 ms per word on consumer GPUs and includes streaming, data-generation, training, calibration, and evaluation tools.

Right: the loop that runs after every recognised word. The judge scores each scene object, the probabilities are calibrated, and the robot commits, waits for the next word or asks which object is meant. The evaluation feeds generated words to the judge directly, without speech recognition.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io
authors: Xiaoman Li, Zhiqiang Yang, Jiayu Hu, Jipeng Kong, Yang Zhang, Jingwei Zhang, Fangzheng Yan, Chunhua Shen, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality long-horizon demonstrations containing detours, failures, hesitations, and imperfect recoveries.
Builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over successful and failed intervention-assisted rollouts.
Uses reverse graph search to estimate minimal remaining steps and reweight chunks by their reduction in this potential.
Reuses recoverable segments and intervention paths without reward models, critics, progress predictors, trajectory comparisons, or progress labels.
Evaluated on four manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, reaching 91% success after a few offline iterations.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.

papers.abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}
authors: Zeji Yi, Soham Dasgupta, Xinyang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath, Guannan Qu, Xi Chen, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Compares continuous and discrete single-step regression and multi-step flow policies in single-task and multi-task training, across simulation and real hardware.

Iterative computation in discrete flows and classifier-free guidance improve responsiveness within predicted action chunks.
Geometric corruption processes inspired by continuous flow matching do not consistently improve discrete policies.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ObjDream. We introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework for robust manipulation. Unlike prior VLA models (a), which primarily rely on image-level understanding and entangled object representations, ObjDream (b) introduces explicit object-level representations and future object state prediction. This object-centric formulation improves manipulation robustness, leading to stronger performance than baseline methods (c).

Figure 2: Overview of the ObjDream architecture. The model integrates three main components: (1) a spatio-temporal object encoder that constructs factorized object slots by separately representing persistent object identity and time-varying object state; (2) an object-level dynamics module that decodes current object states and predicts action-conditioned future object states; and (3) a flow-matching action expert that predicts robot action chunks. ObjDream enhances object-level understanding through factorized object representations and future object state modeling, enabling more generalizable language-conditioned manipulation under object and scene variations.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Atomic-WAM overview. At decision step t, the reasoner predicts an atomic-motion description d̂t from the task instruction l and visual context ot−h:t, where each multi-view observation is formed by concatenating the wrist, left, and right camera views. The WAM conditions on d̂t, ot, and st to generate video latents x̂v and actions x̂a. The lower frames show selected decision steps from a full-task rollout, beginning at Start (t = 0).

Fig. 4: Closed-loop execution-grounded reasoner training. The reasoner samples four candidate atomic motions from a shared observation, while the frozen WAM executes them independently. An evaluator scores motion appropriateness and execution success, and the resulting group-normalized advantages update the reasoner. After each sampling round, one of the highest-reward endpoints is randomly selected as the starting state for the next round.

Fig. 2: Atomic-motion data curation. Displacement and gripper events first divide a demonstration into physical clips. We then annotate each clip from three views, then use temporal context to merge adjacent clips and refine their descriptions. Visible grasp details further enrich grasp-related captions. Finally, we check caption correctness and execution success; mismatched captions are revised and checked again.

papers.abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.

papers.abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
authors: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
bullets: Addresses the limited scene coverage of wrist cameras and the low-resolution detail of external views.
Predicts the next interaction region alongside each action chunk, then receives original-resolution crops plus full images.
Built on π₀.₅ in Single and Dual configurations using one or two external stereo cameras with RGB-D inputs.
On four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single and Dual achieve 70.8% and 77.1% success, compared with 52.1% for wrist-equipped π₀.₅.
Matches the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improves performance with distractors, cloth, and far-away objects.

papers.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $\pi_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
authors: Ziyan Liu, Jiting Liu, Weihong Zhong, Wenda Yu, Yeqiu Chen, Jason Li, Xiaojiang Peng, Shuyuan Hu, Kai Wang, Bo Zhao
bullets: Fixed shared parameters can struggle when different robot operations require competing updates.

Coupled generators follow the policy’s dependency structure, letting vision-language updates influence action-side parameter generation.
The framework is trained with the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
It reports gains of up to 16.30% on LIBERO and Meta-World and up to 14% over π₀.₅ in real-world evaluation.

papers.abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
authors: Xiangyi Wei, Hanzhe Yao, Jingwen Shang, Zhenhong Wu, Yang Li, Changbo Wang

Supports checkpoint reuse for equivalent units and composes heterogeneous policies without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
Evaluations on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks report higher complete-task success and verified progress, with better failure containment and lower error propagation than baselines.

papers.abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
authors: Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: The study compares four integration paradigms: Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
World-representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, while 2D semantic representations provide robust gains across paradigms.
No paradigm is universally best; the decoupled MoT Future Expert performs competitively overall and is particularly robust out of distribution.
World modeling consistently helps standard VLM-based policies and improves action-only baselines, especially on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
Decoupled designs are more compatible with pretrained VLAs, with evaluation spanning in-domain, OOD, few-shot, long-horizon, dynamic, and real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$\pi$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$\pi$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$\pi$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$\pi$ also consistently outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun, Ping Luo, Yao Mu
bullets: Targets the high-dimensional, structured action space of bimanual VLA policies, where cross-hand interactions are often implicit.
Represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as separate, interleaved action tokens.
Uses learnable hand-identity embeddings and factorized RoPE to encode hand identity, sequence position, and shared control timing.
On five DexJoCo tasks, average success rises from 31.9% to 51.3% under rand-obj and from 18.3% to 32.3% under rand-full, compared with π₀.₅.
Also consistently outperforms π₀.₅ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

Right: Conditioned on images, language, and robot state, the action expert generates an action chunk from noise. Output tokens are paired by control timestep into joint bimanual commands, without changing the action horizon.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
authors: Qi Chen, Yuwei Wu, Quan Chen, Kunpeng Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun, Zhi Gao, Yunde Jia
bullets: Addresses the costly, poorly scalable need for task-specific robot demonstrations and retraining when adapting VLAs to novel tasks.
Builds a compact, phase-aware video representation using learned visual-token selection and task-relevant queries supervised by phase captions.
Conditions the pretrained VLA policy on the video and query representations to provide task-specific execution guidance while preserving its action-generation backbone.
Experiments on source and unseen target tasks show improved average performance across unseen target groups with comparable source-task performance.
The approach is scoped to cross-task manipulation adaptation guided by human videos; the abstract does not establish broader settings or limitations.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses failures caused by poor decisions about continuing versus intervening during VLA policy execution.
Uses a rollout-trained Critic to assess success prospects, choose intervention times, and select re-entry targets.
Applies Trajectory Retraction to return the robot to a selected point before resuming the same VLA with a fresh observation.
Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of PICES. Step 1: Draw N initial noise samples and construct a perturbed variant of each sample. Step 2: The action expert processes the resulting N(1 + 1) inputs in a single batch under the shared condition C, producing N nominal action chunks and their corresponding perturbed chunks. Step 3: Stepwise action sensitivity G (n) k is computed by comparing each nominal chunk with its perturbed counterparts. Step 4: Compute a sensitivity score Si for each nominal chunk by averaging its sensitivity over the first W steps and use this score to determine its execution horizon hi. PICES retains candidates whose scores are at or below the median and selects the nominal chunk with the longest execution horizon from the pool.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making hyperspectral distinctions usable by a pretrained model without retraining its visual encoder or action decoder.
Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.
Own-token addition improves external category-probe reuse over pooled replacement (0.701 vs. 0.590) under identical residuals and scale.
Grouped tests recover within-category spectral shape, while spectral swaps indicate that own-token composition approximately doubles target-specific recovery after frozen decoding.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.
Trains an open-weight instruction policy with GRPO through a frozen code generator, averaging rewards from five programs per instruction.
Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.
