papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Introduces a unified simulation benchmark covering eight tasks, 1,600 synchronized demonstrations, and task-specific success criteria.
Compares a no-force baseline with six force-integration designs using a shared π0.5 backbone.
Prompt Fusion achieves 35.31% mean simulation success versus 23.25% for the baseline and improves all three task categories.
In real-world tests, Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion reach 63.00% mean success versus 40.00% for the baseline; only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Keqiang Ren, Xuecheng Ye, Hanyu Liu, Zhihua Wang, Tao Jian, Yunsheng Ma, Jiayi Wen, Xinran Li, Zhigong Song
bullets: Addresses motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arms, and hands, plus error accumulation in long-horizon tasks.
Decouples the 29-DoF action space into hand, arm, and mobile-base branches within a Hierarchical Modular Framework.
Uses COMET cross-attention for inter-module coordination and vision-language-model task decomposition to limit temporal error propagation.
Adds full-palm 2D tactile sensing to represent distributed contact signals across modules.
On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
authors: Hanlong Li, Sihan Tan, Takeshi Ashizawa, Benjamin Yen, Kazuhiro Nakadai
bullets: Rewording instructions reduces base OpenVLA success by 38.0 points on LIBERO, despite using semantically equivalent commands.
Test-time prompt ensembling, paraphrase medoids, and confidence-based selection fail to recover the lost performance; aggregation mainly reduces variance while preserving paraphrase bias.
A wrong-instruction probe links paraphrase sensitivity to how much policy success depends on the instruction, with stronger policies losing a smaller fraction.
LoRA training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points versus −32.0 for a matched control, replicating across seeds and OpenVLA-OFT.
The robustness improvement transfers to withheld phrasings without changing the policy’s overall reliance on instructions.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.

figures.caption: Figure 1: VLX-Go architecture and training workflow. (A) Frozen DINOv3 and SigLIP features are concatenated and pooled into 188 visual tokens: 31× (2× 2) for history and 8× 8 for the current frame. A vision–language adapter projects these features into a transformer backbone; temporal/view indicators, instruction tokens, and a learnable action query complete the input. A three-layer MLP decodes the action state into eight robot-centric waypoints. papers.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy's own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace's source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.

papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
bullets: Addresses robustness challenges from extreme lunar illumination and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
Uses an end-to-end vision-language-action policy mapping observations directly to rover control actions.
Trains with safety-aware expert demonstrations generated in a high-fidelity lunar simulation.
Performs competitively with a modular navigation baseline in closed-loop evaluation under unseen disturbances.
Adaptive execution horizons reduce inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates versus fixed horizons in evaluated scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the VLA policy and training. a) Prior to policy training, an RVQ-VAE is trained on expert trajectories from the policy’s training dataset, which then assigns each trajectory in the same dataset a primary and secondary code pair. b) The policy is trained to predict these primary and secondary codes from camera and BEV-map images. The quantized latent vector corresponding to predicted codes is decoded back to an RVQ-discretized trajectory, whose heading angles are refined by continuous offsets. An execution-horizon head predicts a categorical distribution over execution horizons for each curvature bound. At deployment, the maximum curvature demanded for closed-loop trajectory tracking selects the corresponding execution horizon.

papers.abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
authors: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski

papers.abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
authors: Mingxuan Yan, Litian Gong, Dihong Huang, Zhixu Li, Tianyu Zhang, Wenqian Zhang, Hefeifei Jiang, Peihao Li, Jian Zhang, Mengfei Zhao, Yikai Tang, Hai Zhai, Zehao Wang, Ruijian Liang, Yanjia Huang, Lin Shao, Changliu Liu, Kaiyu Hang, Zhiwen Fan, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Jianfei Yang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Benchmarks weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks.
Across three VLAs, approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning, while the best label granularity depends on the approach and model.
Constant-tag fine-tuning further improves mean success after conditioned pretraining, regardless of tagged or untagged inference.
AXIS-Bench provides replayable simulation trajectories with object and contact states for controlled, user-defined quality-label comparisons.
In a real-world experiment, simulation pretraining increased success from 9.6% to 31.7%.

The simulation benchmark evaluates performance after fine-tuning on 24 target tasks, with matched pretraining data, training budgets, and target-task demonstrations within each VLA comparison. The real-world workflow supports user-defined workspaces and tasks by aligning the simulation workspace, re-rendering demonstrations under the target workspace and camera configuration, fine-tuning on real-world target-task demonstrations, and evaluating task success. papers.abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. This requires costly training and iterative sampling, especially for WAMs with an additional visual branch. We introduce $Δ$-flow, which constructs the source from recent history with mild noise rather than from a fixed Gaussian prior. This moves the source closer to the target, reducing transport to a small residual $Δ$ that can be learned efficiently and enables single-step inference. We integrate $Δ$-flow into the VLA policy $π_{0.5}$ and the WAM policies ImageWAM and Fast-WAM. On LIBERO, ImageWAM reaches 90% success in one epoch rather than six, and Fast-WAM reaches 95% in two epochs rather than eight. With LoRA fine-tuning, $π_{0.5}$ exceeds its baseline's five-epoch performance after one epoch. Single-step inference gives $1.54\times$, $2.49\times$, and $4.45\times$ speedups on $π_{0.5}$, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, respectively. It preserves action smoothness, achieving a $4.5\times$ reduction in action jerk compared with one-step Gaussian sampling. $Δ$-flow reaches state-of-the-art generalization performance on LIBERO-Plus. Action-history sources can be applied to pretrained WAM policies without retraining. Replacing the Gaussian action source at inference largely preserves task success with a single sampling step and can slightly improve it. We further study how action representation and visual information in action learning affect history-to-future prediction in $Δ$-flow. These results show that $Δ$-flow is simple yet effective, improving the efficiency and generalization of robot foundation models.
bullets: Targets costly iterative sampling and training in vision-language-action and world-action robot models.
Builds the flow source from recent action and visual history, learning only the residual transition to future actions and states.

Maintains smooth actions, reducing action jerk 4.5× versus one-step Gaussian sampling, and reaches state-of-the-art generalization on LIBERO-Plus.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye, junjie xie, Yujia Song, Junkai Huang, Dapeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the precision, opacity, and data-scarcity challenges of end-to-end low-level action prediction in surgical robotics.
Uses an MLLM for visual understanding, structured explanations, and skill selection, while verified control programs execute actions.
Trains on a state-to-skill dataset augmented with visual and state perturbations, then optimizes correctness, prerequisites, and output validity.
For brain–machine-interface implantation, reaches 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1 on a fixed test set.
Achieves 88.0% task success across 50 closed-loop real-robot trials.

Fig. 1. Multi-MLLM collaborative data-generation pipeline. Starting from raw image, robot-state, instruction, and skill-label samples, the pipeline expands the data through image/text augmentation and constructs structured rationales using three MLLMs. Candidate outputs are filtered by rule-based checks, leaveone-generator-out cross-validation, and human spot inspection before being retained in the final structured dataset.

Fig. 3. Closed-loop decision example for flexible-electrode implantation. At each step, SurgiCLAW receives the current microscopic image, robot state, and operation query, then outputs a structured rationale, an operator-facing answer, and a single atomic-skill call. The example illustrates a typical decision sequence from spatial registration and image-quality correction to needle alignment and final insertion. surgical data: a multi-MLLM data-generation pipeline expands 5,000 state–skill samples into 30,000 structured ones, and a three-reward group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization objective improves skill selection, prerequisite safety, and output parseability. On the fixed test set SurgiCLAW reaches 94.6% accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1, and it completes 88.0% of 50 closed-loop implantation trials. We interpret these results as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of clinical efficacy: the evaluation covers a single high-precision task using phantom and ex-vivo material, and the closed-loop comparisons are constrained by the modest number of paired trials. Whether the safety and interpretability benefits generalize to other tasks, to more stringent clinical conditions, or to long-horizon unattended operation remains to be established.

papers.abstract: Class 8 trucks differ from passenger cars in geometry, dynamics, and maneuvering requirements. As a result, vision-language-action (VLA) models trained for passenger vehicles do not readily transfer to Class 8 trucks, particularly in unstructured scenarios such as accident scenes and construction zones. Rather than training a truck-driving VLA from scratch, we propose an adapt-then-steer strategy that adapts an off-the-shelf VLA to generate trajectories for Class-8 trucks in these challenging scenarios. In the adapt stage, we use NVIDIA's Alpamayo 1.5 as the base model, fine-tuning only its action-generation stack on a few hundred real-world construction and accident-related highway scenarios. In the steer stage, we introduce Flow Velocity Steering (FVS) to further refine the model's predictions while holding the adapted VLA fixed. FVS is a compact, flow-time-conditioned residual module that adds learned corrections to the action-space flow velocity used to update the action sequence at each generation step. In open-loop evaluation on a scenario-disjoint held-out set, targeted fine-tuning more than halves single-candidate average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) over the entire 6.4 s horizon compared to the base model. Using the same targeted demonstrations, FVS further reduces the fine-tuned model's full-horizon ADE and FDE by 13.9% and 16.5%, respectively. At matched data budgets, targeted supervision yields 19-26% lower full-horizon ADE than general truck-driving supervision, while the targeted model remains competitive with a model fine-tuned on approximately 65 times as many general truck-driving scenarios. These results support adapt-then-steer for data-efficient vehicle-domain transfer to Class 8 trucks. Our project website is available at https://truckvla.github.io.
bullets: Class 8 trucks differ substantially from passenger cars, limiting direct transfer of existing VLAs in unstructured scenes such as accidents and construction zones.
The method fine-tunes only the action-generation stack of NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 1.5, then applies Flow Velocity Steering (FVS), a residual correction module for action-sequence generation.
On a scenario-disjoint open-loop test set, targeted fine-tuning more than halves full-horizon ADE and FDE versus the base model.
FVS further lowers ADE by 13.9% and FDE by 16.5% relative to the fine-tuned model.
Targeted supervision outperforms equally sized general truck-driving supervision and remains competitive with training on roughly 65× more general scenarios.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human demonstrations offer an accessible source of task experience, but differences in body scale and controller response, together with missing robot states, limit their value as humanoid training supervision. We present EgoAlign, a data-construction framework that converts these demonstrations into action and state supervision compatible with a general-purpose, continuous whole-body controller, without collecting physical-robot demonstrations. Using the target-robot model and simulator, EgoAlign guides demonstration collection through execution feedback. It preserves locomotion references for visually guided periodic stepping while adapting upper-body interaction geometry through scale alignment and controller-in-the-loop refinement. A final causal replay reconstructs the corresponding robot states and motion-token labels for training with the human observations. We assess the resulting supervision by fine-tuning a vision--language--action model solely on adapted human demonstrations and deploying it zero-shot on a physical humanoid. The resulting policies perform long-range object relocation, navigation to unseen goal positions, and independently evaluated foot interaction. Refinement improves simulated hand alignment and physical pickup success over kinematic alignment alone, while human collection reduces on-site acquisition time relative to teleoperation. https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/EgoAlign/
bullets: Addresses body-scale, controller-response, and missing-state mismatches between human demonstrations and humanoid training needs.

Applies controller-in-the-loop refinement and causal replay to reconstruct robot states and motion-token labels.
A vision–language–action model trained only on adapted human data transfers zero-shot to a physical humanoid for long-range relocation, navigation, and foot interaction.
Refinement improves simulated hand alignment and physical pickup success over kinematic alignment, while human collection reduces on-site acquisition time versus teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models offer unprecedented generalization for autonomous robots; however, their real-world deployment is frequently bottlenecked by unreliable execution and the prohibitive computational cost of fine-tuning for specific robot embodiments and tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose WayFinder, an end-to-end, closed-loop hierarchical VLA framework that circumvents the need for fine-tuning by decoupling high-level task reasoning from low-level kinematic control. WayFinder utilizes a zero-shot, offboard Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) policy to process linguistic context and state maps for strategic waypoint generation. Asynchronously, a lightweight, onboard policy executes real-time kinematic control at high frequency based on continuous sensor feedback. We evaluate WayFinder in Microsoft AirSim, testing on four environments of varying complexity and three MLLM scales to balance prediction efficacy with computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that WayFinder achieves superior navigation reliability compared to baseline low-level policies. By querying the high-level MLLM only during navigation failures, WayFinder eliminates the need for fine-tuning, minimizes expensive inferences, and significantly increases navigation success rates by up to 27.45%.
bullets: Addresses unreliable execution and costly embodiment- or task-specific VLA fine-tuning.
Uses an offboard MLLM to generate strategic waypoints from language and state maps.
Runs a lightweight onboard controller asynchronously at high frequency using sensor feedback.
Evaluated in AirSim across four environments and three MLLM scales.
Reports improved navigation reliability, with success rates increasing by up to 27.45% by re-querying the MLLM after failures.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
authors: Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Jiawei Zhou, Yuzhang Shang, Emilio Ferrara
bullets: Agentic robots repeatedly invoke an LLM over the full interaction history, causing cost to grow with primitive count.
ChunkAct launches a chained chunk after each sub-goal decision and returns control to the planner only when the chunk fails.
Offline compilation converts memory into executable chunks, allowing memory-free test-time execution.
On LIBERO-Pro, it improves task success by 5.0 points while using 2.9× fewer LLM calls, 4.4× fewer input tokens, and 2.3× fewer output tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ChunkAct introduces action chunking to agentic robotics, improving both task success and efficiency. Bottom: ChunkAct invokes the planner once to launch an action chunk, which executes autonomously and returns a typed error only upon failure. Right: ChunkAct gains both task success and efficiency.

Figure 3: The two stages of ChunkAct. Left: offline, ChunkAct internalizes memory by compiling it into executable action chunks. Right: online, the LLM planner invokes ChunkAct via a single function call, which executes an entire action chunk autonomously and returns a typed error code to the planner only upon failure.

The can is grasped successfully but slips during transport, so ChunkAct returns the error code. The planner interprets this feedback, re-localizes the can, and invokes ChunkAct again, which completes the task.

papers.abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $\pi_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
authors: Gennady Sidorov, Valerii Kornilov, Denis Grankin, Polina Fedotova, Aleksey Postnikov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of building one model for robots with different bodies and action formats.
Uses a shared anatomical action space covering 20 robot families and trains jointly in visual, action-conditioned, and world-action modes.
Separates an action expert from the generator to derive policies, including a distilled single-step policy for real-time control.
Achieves top-tier WorldArena 1.0 world-model accuracy and strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-plus, CALVIN, and LIBERO.
Real-robot adaptation to a humanoid outperforms the cited adapted baselines; specialization and retaining world-model modes improve robustness.

The task instruction, the multi-camera canvas and the robot’s native joint state at 𝑡 = 0 enter a frozen reasoner, a trained generator for the video tokens and, in the adapted policy, an action expert for the state and action tokens, all sharing multimodal attention (the Cosmos 3 Edge mixture of transformers); the layout’s codec maps the native joints to the 79 anatomical slots before the shared input projection (Figure 4). In GreenWAM the state and action tokens pass through the generator; the action expert is split off it for policy adaptation (Section 6.1). papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
authors: Chenru Wen, Huajian Zeng, Haokai Ding, Jian Kang, Anqing Duan, Dawei Zhou, Dezhen Song, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses manipulation failures caused by object slip and visual occlusion without retraining the VLA backbone.
Uses a candidate-conditioned world model to forecast common-horizon outcomes for Commit, Reobserve, and Replan.
A shared task-progress head selects whether to intervene and which recovery action to use, without a failure detector or intervention threshold.
On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, pooled success increased from 13.3% to 30.0% for the frozen π₀.₅ policy.
Transferred to two additional VLA backbones and improved real-robot success under clean and visibility-limited conditions after candidate-rollout adaptation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Haomin Wang, Anqiong Ji, Ke Wang, Zhongshan Liu, Ru Ying, Ran Zheng, Zhipeng Zhang

papers.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.
authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented world models that handle modalities and functions through separate interfaces or modules.
Uses modality-specific encoders and decoders around a shared Unified Dynamics Transformer that jointly evolves RGB, metric depth, and action representations.
Supports joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics.
A motion probe indicates that frozen visual representations retain recoverable action-related motion information.
Trained on heterogeneous egocentric-video, real-robot, and simulation data; the abstract reports top results on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad, and WorldArena.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Overview of the Data Factory producer–consumer pipeline. Heterogeneous multimodal data are organized into episode-centric catalogs Ei = (Vi, Si, Ai, Li,Σi,Λi) and accessed lazily through a SQLite offset index. The model specifies each training sample as qj = (ej , I V j , ISj , I A j , ILj ), including within-source window and modality selection, while source-level sampling controls the mixture of data sources across batches and ranks. The resulting samples are adapted, collated, and asynchronously prefetched into a rank-local ready-batch queue with occupancy 0 ≤ qt ≤ Q, from which the training process consumes prepared batches. The effective pipeline throughput is bounded by λeff ≤ min(λp, λc), where λp and λc denote the producer and consumer rates.
Figure 7: Depth data pipeline. We generate depth pseudo-labels for egocentric and robot videos, filter low-quality clips, and align the retained depth with RGB frames for world model training.

Figure 2: Multimodal encoding and decoding pipelines. RGB video, metric depth, and action are mapped into the unified latent space through modality-specific encoders and processed back into their respective output spaces through modality-specific decoders. The frozen Qwen3-VL-2B converts the structured prompt into the conditioning sequence hund, while robot identity is provided through learnable tokens r. The decoder stage predicts the flow-matching velocity field for each modality rather than directly producing decoded samples.

Figure 11: Overview of Motion Probe. (a) Offline visual motion teacher construction: SpatialTrackerV2 extracts 3D point trajectories from ground-truth RGB video, motion-aware filtering and median aggregation produce a robust visual center trajectory, and a per-window Sim(3) transform aligns it with the recorded end-effector motion. The aligned teacher is frozen and cached. (b) Probing the frozen UDT: a lightweight Motion Head predicts end-effector displacement from the shared video representation. The UDT weights remain frozen, and only the Motion Head is trained. Low probe error indicates that the shared representation encodes action-relevant motion.

Figure 3: Attention pattern of the UDT during pretraining. Self-attention provides cross-modal interaction among RGB, depth, and action, while cross-attention provides the dedicated task-conditioning path from the prompt representation. Depth interacts asymmetrically with the other generative streams during pretraining.

Figure 4: Attention pattern of the UDT during post-training. Compared with pretraining, the geometric stream is opened to bidirectional interaction with RGB and action, enabling multimodal refinement under reliable depth supervision.
Figure 13: Official screenshot of the WorldOlympiad robotics leaderboard, where our proposed model ranks first.
Figure 5: Function modes of Thinker-WM. Each panel shows the modality configuration of one function, with dashed outlines indicating omitted inputs or outputs.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots performing outdoor deliveries must interpret complex scenes, anticipate changes, and navigate in socially compliant ways. Robot demonstrations are costly to collect at the scale needed for generalization. Egocentric web videos offer abundant human navigation experience, but differences in viewpoint and motion make this experience difficult to transfer to robots. We introduce DR-VLA, a Mixture-of-Transformers framework that transfers human navigation experience through a domain-invariant scene representation (DISR). The framework combines vision-language understanding and latent world modeling with a flow-matching action expert. We introduce EgoLynx, comprising 10,000 hours of curated egocentric web video (EgoLynx-Web) and 2,000 clips of teleoperated robot navigation collected during real-world deliveries (EgoLynx-Robot). We pretrain the understanding and world experts on EgoLynx-Web without action labels, then adapt the model to robot observations and train the action expert on EgoLynx-Robot to predict executable trajectories. We also propose the Quadruped Navigation Score (QNS), a pseudo-closed-loop metric combining safety, instruction compliance, comfort, and progress. On the held-out EgoLynx-Robot test split, DR-VLA improves QNS by approximately 5% and reduces open-loop final heading error (FHE) by 14.6%, each relative to the best competing result for that metric. Ablations show that web-video pretraining improves generalization and that the model's key components contribute to performance. As a future-prediction target, DISR outperforms five generic visual representations and yields performance close to task-specific 3D perception without dedicated geometric labels or point clouds for target construction. Trained separately on NAVSIM v1 without web pretraining, DR-VLA achieves 92.1 PDMS, suggesting that the framework also applies to autonomous driving.

bullets: Addresses the scarcity and domain mismatch of robot demonstrations for socially compliant outdoor navigation.

papers.abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as $\pi_{0.5}$, have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities by scaling behavior cloning across massive datasets. However, these models frequently suffer from distributional convergence, a phenomenon where the policy regresses to "safe" but suboptimal mean behaviors due to mode averaging in the training data. This often results in generic grasp strategies, Convergent Defaults, that fail in constrained or long-tail scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel framework to identify and correct these behaviors without parameter updates. We introduce a three-stage methodology: (1) Probing for Defaults, identifying task-specific mode collapse; (2) Diagnostic Root Cause Analysis, utilizing the VLA's latent reasoning capabilities to verbalize the logic behind suboptimal actions; and (3) Structured Guidance Injection, where concrete, distinct alternatives are encoded into reusable "Lens Prompts" that shift the sampling distribution. We validate this approach using $\pi_{0.5}$ in ManiSkill3 simulation environments. We hypothesize that our method outperforms vanilla $\pi_{0.5}$ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by effectively breaking convergent defaults in complex manipulation tasks.
authors: Mohammed Daba (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China), Waleed Abdulrahman Saleh AlAkwa (University of Sana'a, Sana'a, Yemen)
bullets: Targets distributional convergence in behavior-cloned VLA models, where mode averaging produces safe but suboptimal “Convergent Defaults.”
Probes task behavior to identify task-specific mode collapse.

Evaluated with π₀.₅ in ManiSkill3 simulations; the abstract states a hypothesis of improvement over vanilla π₀.₅ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting, not confirmed results.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The Diagnostic Lens Framework. We treat the VLA as a reasoning engine to diagnose its own action priors. By extracting the root cause of a default behavior, we construct a textual ”Lens” that reshapes the flow matching distribution during inference.

Fig. 1. Breaking the Convergent Default. VLA models often regress to the mean of their training data, causing failures in constrained environments. Our method identifies these modes and injects structured guidance (Lens) to shift the action distribution toward expert behaviors.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.
authors: Shangqing Zhou, Zhennan Jiang, Ning Ma, Xin Fu, Yupeng Zheng, Shuai Tian, Huangrui Li, Jiahao Liu, Chao Yu, Zhongpu Xia, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao

Applies chunk-wise action noise to preserve exploration while limiting prediction-degrading jitter.
Trains long-horizon tasks stage by stage using resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling.
Reports higher success than SFT on RoboTwin and six real-robot tasks; phone-packaging success increases from 30% to 75%.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang

Shows zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive without specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. We study this human--VLA communication gap by separating an \emph{information gap}, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, from a residual \emph{execution gap}, where even a fully specified task depends on how it is organized and invoked. To do this, we characterize how people naturally express demonstrated objectives and evaluate controlled variants of the same physical tasks, with detailed analysis on $\pi_{0.5}$ and consistent trends on $\pi_0$-FAST and Cosmos3-Edge. Our study reveals that humans increasingly compress instructions as tasks grow, relying more on contextual grounding and implicit execution structure. Current policies are misaligned with this behavior: they tolerate grounding dependence relatively well, but struggle when task semantics or event structure must be reconstructed. Even after the information gap is resolved, execution remains sensitive to command granularity and invocation state. These findings identify concrete targets for human-centered policy learning and interfaces that better bridge natural human objectives to robot behavior. Project website: https://commgap.github.io/.
bullets: Separates the communication gap into an information gap—unresolved semantics, grounding, or event structure—and an execution gap involving task organization and invocation.
Analyzes how humans describe demonstrated objectives and evaluates controlled variants of the same physical tasks across several policies.
Finds that people compress instructions more as tasks become complex, relying increasingly on context and implicit execution structure.
Policies handle grounding dependence relatively well but struggle to reconstruct task semantics and event structure.
Even fully specified tasks remain sensitive to command granularity and invocation state, motivating human-centered policy learning and interfaces.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Human–VLA communication gap. For the same physical task, human specifications vary in task content, reference, and composition, producing substantially different VLA performance (top). We separate this mismatch into an information gap, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, and a residual execution gap, where the fully resolved task remains sensitive to command organization and invocation state (bottom), distinguishing recovering the intended task from reliably executing it through the policy’s learned interface.

Fig. 6: From human specifications to measurable information gaps. The same physical objective can be expressed through substantially different human specifications. Our taxonomy classifies each instruction by its task content, reference form, and composition, and maps these choices to the executable information made available to the policy: which actions, objects, and destinations are directly specified, require grounding, or are omitted. This yields quantitative measures of semantic coverage, groundedness, and decomposition ratio. Rather than studying instructions only as lexical variants, we can therefore relate VLA performance to the information they carry and identify which missing structure the policy can recover and which it cannot.

Fig. 4: Residual execution gap. On the same fully specified Action–Direct– Enumerated tasks, issuing atomic events sequentially improves success and partial progress over a single upfront prompt for all three policies, and resetting the arm to its home configuration between events adds a further gain.

Fig. 3: Behavioral cost of unresolved task structure. Left: For all three policies, grounding dependence is cheap, while missing action/object/destination information and undecomposed events cost far more. Right: With task complexity, coverage and decomposition become more strongly associated with the success gap than groundedness.

Fig. 2: Humans increasingly compress execution structure as tasks grow. Instruction length increases with the number of events (left), but the executable structure made explicit decreases (right): coverage declines moderately, while groundedness and decomposition fall sharply.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide
bullets: Addresses the cost of manually annotating language-conditioned robotic navigation and reasoning.
Uses an open-source VLM as both a self-teacher and student policy; the teacher infers navigation goals and reasoning from privileged trajectory feedback.
The student uses onboard observations to predict future ego-frame trajectories and describe scene semantics, plans, and reasoning.
Evaluated on 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks.
Reports 30% higher success than the strongest baseline indoors and on multi-stage tasks, plus 95% success on outdoor tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Reasoning Legibility. Figure 2: Action Self-Distillation. A single pre-trained VLM is used as both the self-teacher πϕ and student πθ . During training, the self-teacher receives privileged information by projecting the ground-truth future trajectory y onto the front-view observation as o∗0, enabling it to infer a language goal ĝ and scene-grounded reasoning trace R. The student observes only deployable inputs o0 and learns to match the teacher’s reasoning tokens with a KL loss, while predicting future trajectory tokens τ̃0:H with a cross-entropy loss against the ground-truth trajectory y. The teacher weights are updated as an EMA of the student.

papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
authors: Jack Lu, Yurong You, Boyi Li, Yulong Cao, Thomas Tian, Chaowei Xiao, Xiangyu Chen, Wenjie Luo, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Yan Wang
bullets: Reasoning text improves the VLA backbone, even when the action expert does not attend to the reasoning generated during the current call.
For long-horizon tasks, reasoning can be generated during execution and used as episodic memory rather than delaying action.
Across four manipulation and driving benchmarks, TacitVLA matches explicit-reasoning performance with up to 3.4× lower latency.
It matches the latency of non-reasoning training while achieving up to 17.1% higher success.
It reports strong results on RoboMME Counting, RMBench, LIBERO-Plus, and PhysicalAI-AV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TacitVLA retains the benefit of reasoning supervision without conditioning its actions on the generated text. Left: how the policies act in one call. Given the context 𝑐𝑡, on memory tasks including the ledger 𝑀𝑡 of past subtasks, the backbone generates the reasoning 𝑟𝑡 and conditions the action expert that outputs the action chunk 𝑎𝑡. In Explicit Reasoning, the action expert attends to 𝑟𝑡, so every action chunk waits for it. TacitVLA trains on the same sequence with 𝑟𝑡 masked from the action expert, bypassing the need to generate 𝑟𝑡 on non-memory tasks. On memory tasks, 𝑟𝑡 still becomes the next ledger entry (dashed loop), but is generated asynchronously during execution instead of making the action expert wait. No Reasoning is the same architecture trained without reasoning supervision. Right: TacitVLA matches Explicit Reasoning’s success at 1.7× and 3.4× lower latency, andmatches No Reasoning’s latency at +3.5% and+5.3% success (Tables 3, 5, 15).

Figure 3: TacitVLA matches the latency of No Reasoning on every benchmark, and Explicit Reasoning’s latency is 1.4× to 3.4× higher. Each bar is one policy’s latency per call: 𝑇action for No Reasoning and TacitVLA, and 𝑇action + 𝑇reason for Explicit Reasoning, whose actions wait for text generation. The ratio above each group is Explicit Reasoning’s latency over TacitVLA’s. On the memory tasks, TacitVLA generates the ledger entry during execution, taking at most 23% of the execution window, so the next call never waits for generation. All values are means over model calls on one H100, with the per-stage breakdown in Table 15 (Appendix C).

Figure 2: Training and deployment of Explicit Reasoning and TacitVLA. The two policies share the training sequence and differ in one attention-mask cell, which decouples TacitVLA’s actions from text generation at deployment. (a) The backbone predicts the reasoning 𝑟𝑡 and the tokenized actions ?̃?𝑡 (an auxiliary target) under cross-entropy, and the action expert denoises the action chunk 𝑎𝑡 under flow matching. (b) Rows attend to columns. The backbone is causal. The action expert attends to 𝑐𝑡 and its own action chunk, to 𝑟𝑡 only in Explicit Reasoning, and never to ?̃?𝑡. The crossed cell is that difference. (c) On non-memory tasks, Explicit Reasoning needs to generate 𝑟𝑡 before denoising and executing the action chunk, while TacitVLA does not. Onmemory tasks, both generate the ledger entry 𝑟𝑡: Explicit Reasoning before action execution, TacitVLA during it concurrently.
