papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa, Takehiko Ohkawa, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Shigeo Morishima, Kei Ota
bullets: Addresses costly, difficult-to-reproduce real-robot policy evaluation through real-to-sim simulation.
Combines 200° fisheye capture, 3DGS reconstruction, 3D foundation-model object modeling, and MuJoCo simulation.
Benchmarks two bimanual platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and two pi0.5-based policies, reproducing real-world policy ordering in 8 of 9 scene-task comparisons.
Tests policy sensitivity to ceiling holes, floaters, warping, and capture disturbances, and examines whether novel-view quality predicts ranking reliability.
Finds task-dependent effects and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction; no general scene-acceptance rule is established.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | YUBI-Real2Sim pipeline. We capture the background with a single 200◦ FOV camera, estimate camera poses with COLMAP, and densify the point cloud with OpenMVS to initialize Gaussian Wrapping for high-fidelity reconstruction. We generate object geometry and textures with TRELLIS 2.0 and approximate collision meshes with CoACD. The reconstructed scene and objects are integrated into MuJoCo simulation. For wrist-view rendering, we independently render the background Gaussians and the MuJoCo visual meshes, then composite their pixels using depth maps.

Figure 3 | Simulated scenes, and the added disturbances for 3DGS or viewpoints. One column per scene, one band per condition. Blue: the clean 3DGS reconstructions the rollouts run in. Red: the same reconstructions carrying a counterfactual artifact — a ceiling hole in FR3 Flat, the 54◦ and 90◦ half-angles either side of the dashed rule, low floaters in FR3 Duo, and warping in TX-G2. Amber, the colour Fig. 1 gives capture: one reduced-coverage reconstruction per condition, each in the scene of its column. The panels show representative examples of the reconstruction conditions. We evaluated two task-specific VLA checkpoints for each of three tasks (Cup, Tape, and Pen) in all three scenes (FR3 Flat, FR3 Duo, and TX-G2).

Figure 4 | Policy ranking in real and simulated evaluation. Black/gray bars show real success and blue bars show simulated success; light and dark bars denote π1 and π2, respectively, as in Fig. 1. Policy labels are fixed within each task across scenes and domains. Error bars are marginal 95% Wilson confidence intervals from 20 real and 80 simulated trials per policy. The observed ranking agrees in 8/9 scene–task pairs (88.9%); Flat Cup is reversed.

Figure 1 | YUBI-Real2Sim analyzes and verifies 3DGS scenes for reliable policy-ranking evaluation. The quality of 3DGS can easily degrade depending on the camera views. We analyze how variations in 3DGS quality affect policy rankings and examine whether scene-quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability.

Table I | Effect of each counterfactual (CF) condition on the nine scene–task policy comparisons. Significance: comparisons whose Fisher-test status (p < 0.05) is lost or gained relative to Clean; the others keep their status. Ranking vs. Clean: comparisons whose simulated ranking is reversed or tied relative to Clean. Agreement with real: comparisons whose simulated ranking matches the real ranking. Clean agrees in 8/9 (Flat Cup is reversed) and no CF condition corrects it, so every reversal or tie is a lost agreement.

papers.abstract: We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems. Project website: https://embodied-astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied-astra-robomme.
authors: Jack B. Jedlicki, Amish Sethi, Heng Yang

papers.title: Can a Frontier VLM Serve as a Robot Policy for Memory-Dependent Manipulation?

papers.abstract: Household robots must successfully navigate im-perfect circumstances, both in their internal models and the external world. We introduce a benchmark of seven long-horizon household tasks in Habitat that vary initial robot memory and environment configurations. We evaluate adaptations of ReAct, VLM-TAMP, and Tru-POMDP within a shared execution framework across 90 tasks-environment-memory combinations, totaling 1,350 episodes. Our evaluation measures task success, partial completion, and action efficiency, along with rule-based analysis of execution traces. ReAct achieves the highest overall task success (45.3%) and completion (71.7%), while having accurate initial memory does not consistently yield the highest performance for every planner. We identify recurring placement errors, precondition errors, and redundant actions through trace analysis. These findings highlight differences in how the evaluated planners use initial knowledge and respond to uncertainty.
authors: Harsh Muriki, Gayathri Aravindan, Yuchen Zheng, Sonia Chernova
bullets: Introduces seven long-horizon household tasks varying robot memory and environment configurations.
Evaluates ReAct, VLM-TAMP, and Tru-POMDP across 90 task–environment–memory combinations and 1,350 episodes.
Measures task success, partial completion, action efficiency, and execution-trace errors.
ReAct achieves the highest reported success (45.3%) and completion (71.7%).
Trace analysis finds recurring placement, precondition, and redundant-action errors; accurate initial memory does not consistently improve performance.

papers.tldr: A Habitat benchmark shows that long-horizon household robot planning remains error-prone under uncertainty, with ReAct performing best overall among three evaluated planners.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: D-World, an explicit world-language-action model. Implicit models (left) keep the world in network weights or predicted video. D-World (right) writes it as an executable twin. SENSE constructs the twin, PLAN proposes trajectories and twin revisions, and a gate checks each action chunk before execution. Measurements of the real robot drive state correction and replay-checked parameter revision (RSI), and the dashed path requests reconstruction. In a bread-grasp episode, the twin shows both grippers open, ACTION shows the robot holding a lifted bread slice, and the measurement pair compares this post-lift observation with the reconstructed twin. In the language channel, PLAN asks and SENSE answers.

Figure 2: Replay-checked revision after a failed lift. In a failed bread grasp, the real bread remains in its rack while the twin lifts it with the gripper. Reducing the modeled thickness reproduces the slip during replay and reduces both the depth and the closure residual. Friction, to which this chunk is insensitive, is left unchanged. The revision passes the non-regression check and is accepted, and the next chunk attempts another grasp without reconstruction. Here j is the latest executed round and t the revision round. An earlier thickness proposal had increased the residual on the preceding chunk and was rejected.

Figure 3: Towel handling. (a) The top row shows camera images and the initial twin rendered from the same cameras, and the bottom row selected interaction and reconstruction stages, numbered by chunk. Dashed outlines mark the grasp mismatch between the twin and the robot, after which reconstruction changes the towel representation to match its observed configuration. (b) Where the time goes in the same episode. SENSE is blue, lighter while it answers a question, PLAN is orange, and the robot’s chunks are green with the numbers of (a). The bottom lanes magnify the three chunks between the two reconstructions. Model inference fills almost the entire hour, whereas the robot moves for seconds per chunk.

Figure 4: From episodes to high-fidelity worlds. (a) Each episode records observations, twins, controls and revisions. (b) Versioned libraries collect agent-written skills, such as perception and motion primitives, and scene bodies from completed episodes, whose parameters RSI has validated against the robot’s measurements. (c) Offline, recorded chunks are replayed jointly to refit parameters, and the refitted twin is rendered again with the same geometry, here in MuJoCo and in Blender. Skills and assets can be reused in later episodes, and refitted twins can serve post-training.

Table 1: Replay residuals before and after parameter revision. Depth entries are absolute signedmedian residuals, maximized over the available cameras. Closure is dimensionless on a scale from 0 (open) to 1 (closed).

papers.selection_reason: Explicit world-language-action model with digital-twin self-improvement for robot manipulation and planning.
papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.tldr: D-World enables robots to improve an explicit, inspectable digital twin through measurement-grounded planning and execution, without updating the underlying LLM.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
authors: Yuqi Ye, Caigao Jiang, Zhuonan Wang, Congyuan Pei, Chao Qu, Changhao Peng, Junhong Lin, Qize Yu, Zetian Song, Guangzhao Fu, Chongruo Wu, Shiyu Huang, Shuchang Zhou, Honggou Yang, Wei Gao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but weakly understood vision-action models and accurate but slow autoregressive VLAs.
Uses joint chain-of-thought supervision to preserve spatial understanding and guide trajectory generation.
Generates actions before chain-of-thought during training, so inference outputs only actions for lower latency.
AUGUstus-GRPO jointly optimizes action and reasoning objectives.
Reports strong performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes, with 12 Hz operation in a preliminary real-vehicle deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of AUGUstus. AUGUstus takes video and ego status as input and uses one shared transformer to first generate clean action and then understand a CoT containing key-object bounding boxes and future position. Action tokens use bidirectional attention and cannot attend to the CoT tokens. At inference, AUGUstus directly outputs the action to ensure low latency.

Figure 3 The pipeline of AUGUstus-GRPO. Paired 𝑥0 actions and autoregressive CoTs share a group-relative advantage, with closed-form JaT-GRPO and token-level CoT-GRPO. Stage I focuses on progress via PDMS reward, while Stage II focuses on safety via terminal and safety rewards.

The three rows are three alternative supervision targets, not a serial pipeline: each is trained alone on the same scene and action, and the model never consumes one row’s output to produce another’s. One pastel outer frame encloses the title, annotated scene, and JSON answer of each CoT variant. (a) Perception CoT: a 2-D box and a class label for every salient agent (vehicle: blue, bicycle: orange, pedestrian: violet) on the 2048 × 512 deployment canvas. (b) Prediction CoT: each box is annotated with its future relative position and a motion arrow; this is the default target. (c) Planning CoT: the ground-truth 4 s trajectory (green) projected onto the camera strip, with a BEV inset (ego-left on the left) showing the top-down right-turn arc.

Figure 1 The difference between AUGUstus and other autonomous-driving VLA paradigms. Our method unifies generation and understanding under AUGUstus-mode, so that joint CoT supervision preserves the VLM’s understanding in the shared representation, yielding safer, more accurate actions with an RL-friendly action distribution and low-latency deployment.

papers.title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding
papers.tldr: AUGUstus unifies diffusion-based action generation with autoregressive chain-of-thought understanding to deliver safer, accurate, and low-latency autonomous-driving planning.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. Yet existing closed-loop benchmarks primarily measure route completion, safety, and rule compliance, leaving a fundamental question unresolved: does language actually determine which feasible behavior the vehicle executes? A trajectory may be safe and successful while still violating or even ignoring the passenger's instruction. To address this, we introduce \ltd, a benchmark designed to directly test this capability. Its key evaluation unit, the paired counterfactual unit (PCU), holds the initial driving scene fixed while changing only the instruction. This design enables us to distinguish isolated instruction success from counterfactual paired success across four instruction-following scopes. To test whether this distinction persists across evaluation regimes, we instantiate Language2Drive in complementary closed-loop CARLA simulation, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks, including our released CARLA-Language2Drive simulator with purpose-built maps. Evaluating representative driving VLAs across these settings reveals a striking mismatch between strong driving competence and weak language control: 93.2% of successful rollouts do not have a successful counterpart under the alternative feasible instruction. This failure is dominated by one-sided completion, where a model repeatedly executes one preferred behavior but fails when the same scene requires the counterfactual alternative. These results expose two fundamental limitations of current evaluation: isolated success and driving scores, which are widely used by conventional driving benchmarks, can substantially overstate language-following capability, while current driving VLAs themselves lack reliable instruction following under matched counterfactual tests.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

A residual predictor refreshed after simulator update supplies no-oracle scores for unpaired recursive chunks and is frozen during imagination and policy optimization. papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by connecting visual perception and language instructions to action generation. However, many manipulation tasks depend on auditory cues that cannot be reliably inferred from visual observations and may need to be elicited through physical interaction. To address this gap, we present ListenVLA, an audio-conditioned VLA policy built on GR00T N1.7 for sound-guided manipulation. ListenVLA combines semantic audio embeddings with waveform-derived acoustic cues over a causal audio history and conditions continuous action generation through audio tokens and feature modulation. Moreover, we introduce an audio-action binding objective that uses context-matched demonstrations to link auditory differences to demonstrated action differences. The objective supervises short-horizon differences between flow-velocity predictions under different audio conditions, with shared pure-noise action inputs and fixed non-audio observations, alongside full-chunk action supervision. Furthermore, we develop LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark covering sound-based target selection, responses to auditory events, and physical interactions that reveal acoustic evidence. Experiments on LIBERO-Audio and three real-world manipulation tasks show excellent performance. Ablation studies support the contributions of binding supervision and audio modulation, while audio swap tests show that sound influences action predictions. Our code and videos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/listenvla-F18D
authors: Jiaqi Fan, Rui Xu, Jiakun Xia, Xuyu Fan, Shuailei Ma, Yuefeng Wang, Qing Wang, Jiarui Zhang, Yili Fu, Xu Li

Introduces audio-action binding supervision using matched demonstrations and short-horizon differences in flow-velocity predictions.
Presents LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark spanning sound-based selection, auditory-event responses, and interactions that reveal acoustic evidence.

papers.abstract: World-action models should preserve the intended manipulation across equivalent descriptions of a spatial goal. We evaluate this consistency in 864 rollouts from three models across four RoboLab scenes, holding initial states and task goals fixed. Describing relations through the reference object rather than the object-to-move lowers the rate of reaching a stable placement by 12.2 percentage points on average. The effect of instruction rephrasing varies across spatial relations, so aggregate scores can hide sensitivity to wording. Standalone tests of the policies' language understanding identify relation reversals and show that adding images can disrupt otherwise correct text-only interpretations. Rollout analysis also distinguishes spatial placement from instruction following: moving the wrong object can satisfy the requested relation, and rates of stable placement fall from 43.2% at any time to 21.8% at episode end. These findings motivate a more thorough evaluation of world-action models' steerability, language understanding, and grounding. Evaluations should test consistency across equivalent instructions, verify that the intended object moved, and check whether the requested arrangement persists to the end of the rollout.
authors: Ali-Adeeb Abbas, Esmaeil Seraj, Behrad Toghi, Taskin Padir
bullets: Evaluates instruction consistency across 864 rollouts, three models, and four RoboLab scenes with fixed initial states and goals.
Reference-object phrasing reduces stable-placement success by 12.2 percentage points on average, with sensitivity varying by spatial relation.
Standalone language tests reveal relation reversals; adding images can disrupt interpretations that are correct from text alone.
Rollout analysis separates spatial placement from instruction following: the wrong object may be moved, and end-of-episode stability is lower than transient success.
Findings call for evaluations that test equivalent instructions, verify object identity, and assess whether arrangements persist to episode end.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly control robots using VLA policies, perception models, and procedural knowledge. These modules are difficult to reuse because their interfaces, embodiment assumptions, and conditions of use differ, and their benefits on physical tasks remain unclear. We package them as embodied skills that extend agent skills with explicit embodiment assumptions and conditions of use, building 250 action, perception, and experience skills from 1,052 resources. On this basis we introduce EmbodiedSkillBench, which runs an agent in a closed observation-action loop and records success, actions, tokens, and wall-clock time. It supports three modes: native control, skill-only execution, and Agent-Directed Reuse (ADR), a mode we propose in which the agent keeps its native controls and decides for each skill whether to invoke, modify, or ignore it. Across four agents on 100 perturbed LIBERO-Pro tasks, we find that skills help an agent only as far as they exceed what it can already do. Skill-only execution lifts GPT-5.6-Sol from 11% to 63% and Kimi-K3 and Claude-Opus-5 by about 20 points, while cutting their token usage by 58% to 85%. Yet all four agents then end up between 61% and 64%, and GPT-6-Astra falls from 92% under native control to 61%. This suggests that as agents grow stronger, the role of embodied skills shifts from supplying missing capability to reducing cost: GPT-6-Astra already solves most tasks through native control, so restricting it to skills removes more than it adds. Under ADR, which lets it keep native control and call skills selectively, GPT-6-Astra recovers to 85%, within 7 points of native control, while using 14.1% fewer tokens and 11.9% less time. With Jev as a skill choosing motion directions and gripper actions, it reaches 81% with 50% fewer tokens and 57% less time. The code is available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/EmbodiedSkill-Bench.
authors: Zhi Han, Zihan Guo, Chenxi Zeng, Zicai Cui, Yue Xin, Ming Zhou, Dongzhan Zhou, Weinan Zhang, Yang Li
bullets: Benchmarks embodied skills—action, perception, and experience modules—with explicit embodiment assumptions and usage conditions.
Evaluates agents in a closed observation-action loop across native control, skill-only execution, and Agent-Directed Reuse (ADR).
On 100 perturbed LIBERO-Pro tasks, skill-only execution improves weaker agents but constrains the strongest agent, reducing its success from 92% to 61%.
ADR lets the strongest agent retain native control while selectively using skills, recovering 85% success with 14.1% fewer tokens and 11.9% less time.
The benchmark includes 250 skills built from 1,052 resources and measures success, actions, token usage, and wall-clock time.

papers.title: Embodied Skill Bench: Benchmarking How Well Agents with Embodied Skills Perform on Physical Tasks

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction enable the extraction of temporally consistent 3D motion from RGB observations; however, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models still predominantly rely on 2D image-text priors. Therefore, they do not accurately represent the fundamental dynamics of the 3D world associated with physical actions. This over-reliance on static 2D visual cues limits the capacity of VLA models in achieving robust robot manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce FlowVLA, a reconstruction-guided, pluggable 3D flow learning framework aimed at empowering VLA models with an inherent understanding of action-relevant dynamics. Instead of requiring explicit 3D sensor inputs or altering the inference-time architecture, our method is designed to utilize temporally aligned 3D flow only during training. This allows the model to learn the dynamic evolution of the physical scene while preserving the computational efficiency of conventional 2D VLA backbones. To bridge scene-level dynamics with robotic manipulation, we propose a modular 3D flow learning framework with dual-level flow supervision. Specifically, point-level flow guides the model to forecast the future displacements of task-critical 3D points, while TCP-level flow aggregates these motions to align with the robot's TCP trajectories. This dual-level flow supervision encourages the model to focus on semantically meaningful dynamic regions, effectively coupling scene-level motion with precise control signals. Extensive evaluations across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that FlowVLA consistently improves manipulation performance, zero-shot robustness, and optimizes data efficiency. FlowVLA adds only lightweight auxiliary heads during training and discards them at inference. Therefore, FlowVLA introduces no additional 3D sensor inputs, architectural modifications, or inference-time computation.
authors: Junhyeong Go, Mingyu Jung, Woobin Im, Jongbin Ryu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of VLA models relying mainly on static 2D image-text priors for physical-world dynamics.
Uses temporally aligned 3D flow from reconstructed RGB observations only during training.
Applies dual-level supervision: point-level flow predicts task-critical 3D point motion, while TCP-level flow aligns scene motion with robot control trajectories.
Adds lightweight auxiliary heads that are discarded at inference, preserving conventional 2D VLA efficiency.
Simulation and real-world evaluations show improved manipulation performance, zero-shot robustness, and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $\pi_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $\pi_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model-memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.
authors: Seongmin Park, Jaewon Lee, Yujun Heo, Yoonsik Kim, Seheon Choi, Hyoung-rock Kim, Jungwook Choi
bullets: Quantization reduces VLA deployment costs but can impair long-horizon completion and robustness to visual and semantic shifts.
Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, QAT generally outperforms PTQ yet remains below full precision.
QCRL combines progress-based advantage estimation, FP rollout references, and quantization-aware source conditioning.
Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP mean score with INT4 W4A16 and 100.7% with NVFP4 W4A4 on evaluated settings.
The reported deployments achieve 42.9% model-memory savings or a 1.73× speedup, depending on the quantization format.

papers.abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.
authors: Abdollah Pourasghari, Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour, Mohammad Roustaei
bullets: The dataset contains 258 instances from 230 real household and office photographs, with reference plans, ambiguity/infeasibility labels, disambiguation QA pairs, and generated rationales.
Experiments ablate retrieval augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and agentic disambiguation, using LLM judging and the new PGOS-FA metric.
Retrieval augmentation has the strongest and most robust effect; finer-grained additions are directionally positive but inconclusive at this dataset scale.
PGOS-FA incorporates step-order sensitivity, over-generation penalties, and Persian-adapted embeddings, and correlates with human judgments at least as well as the LLM judge.

The benchmark and best configuration outperform an independently reproduced external baseline despite using a weaker backbone; results are limited by the small dataset and single-backbone ablation scale.

papers.abstract: Open-world mobile manipulation requires a robot to find an object, approach it, and move it to a target receptacle from a language instruction. Training vision-language model (VLM) agents for these tasks requires demonstrations of both action selection and active vision. Existing pipelines often convert planned trajectories into high-level action labels, but shortest-path progress provides limited supervision for deciding where to look. We introduce Agent-Interface Data Alignment (AIDA), a data collection pipeline in which a teacher directly selects and executes actions through the deployed agent's skill interface. For mobile manipulation, we design teachers that maintain target visibility, recover lost targets, and approach for picking or placing. We add template-based spatial reasoning supervision and use a shared harness to organize observations, history, and outputs during training and inference. The resulting agent, AIDA-OWMM, achieves 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out OWMM episodes. Teacher sensitivity analysis shows that active-vision demonstrations improve student success. The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training. Applying AIDA to a navigation subset of EmbodiedBench further demonstrates the pipeline's utility for navigation tasks.
authors: Ronghe Qiu, Teli Ma, Jiaming Zhou, Zeying Gong, Yiting He, Qiang Huang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Targets open-world tasks requiring object search, approach, pickup, and placement from language instructions.
Collects teacher demonstrations through the agent’s actual skill interface, including maintaining and recovering target visibility.
Adds template-based spatial-reasoning supervision and a shared harness for organizing observations, history, and outputs.
AIDA-OWMM reaches 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out simulation episodes; active-vision demonstrations improve performance.
The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.
bullets: Addresses inference latency that grows with action-sequence length in autoregressive VLA models.
Uses shared vision and frozen text encoders, discrete skill selection, a JEPA latent-state predictor, and flow matching for action-chunk generation.
Analyzes representation-collapse regularization and latent sub-goal thresholding to limit error accumulation across task phases.
On LIBERO-10, a two-camera policy achieved 40.0% success over 200 episodes in a preliminary single-run evaluation.
The model has under 20M trainable parameters; a single-camera decision step took 10–14 ms on an Apple M4.

figures.caption: Figure 2: High-level architectural overview of the Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA) framework. Multimodal observations are projected into latent and text embeddings that condition the selection of an active primitive ut, the forecast of the next latent state ẑt+1 and its uncertainty σt+1 by a JEPA predictor, and a continuous flow-matching solver that generates an action chunk At, of which an uncertainty-dependent prefix of length Ht is executed.

Figure 5: Planned Closed-Loop Evaluation in Simulation (Future Work). To benchmark high-frequency reactive control, the Goal-Conditioned VPA framework will be deployed in GPU-accelerated simulators subjected to dynamic physical and visual perturbations. High-frequency sensory streams are processed by the VPA pipeline, whose sequential depth of K + 3 network evaluations per decision step is independent of the action horizon (Proposition 5.1), and the resulting action chunks are executed open-loop for an uncertainty-dependent number of steps Ht. This setting is intended to test, under realistic closed-loop conditions, whether VPA avoids the low inference rates reported for autoregressive VLA architectures, such as about 1–5 Hz for RT-2 [1]. Because the simulator exposes the privileged physical state yt, the evaluation will also log the quantities required to test the conditional analysis of Section 5.3.

During this stage, the predictor is conditioned on the discrete primitive labels ut supplied by logged demonstration trajectories (Eq. 10); the frozen text encoder is not involved. At the end of the stage, Eψ and Pω are frozen, which fixes the latent scale γ̄⋆ and the deployment threshold τ⋆ (Eq. 9).

papers.title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors

papers.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboCombine.
authors: Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Full-instruction training appears to memorize seen sequence templates: 40.0% success on covered combinations versus 7.7% on recombinations.
HSE diagnoses failures across planning, triggering, and policy execution through a shared modular interface.
RoboCombine evaluates skill recombination without combined-skill training trajectories using ordered-success and transition-conversion metrics.
Failures cluster at subtask boundaries, revealing a start state gap between canonical starts and handoff states.
PRTI broadens atomic-task initialization and reaches 18.16% ordered success under oracle-timed HSE, outperforming the reported perturbation and reset baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
authors: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Uses a trained message channel and per-arm diffusion action heads on frozen VLA backbones with decentralised execution.
Communication is valuable mainly under partial observability, such as an occluded handover where only one agent sees the box marker.
With shared overhead-camera views, disabling messages has little effect on two- and three-arm handover performance.
On a wrist-only variant, messages improve success from 64.3% to 74.8%; on the occluded tray task, success is 76.0% with messages versus 1.3% when removed during training.
CoLA generalises across VLA backbones and matches a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline while using fewer trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1 CoLA framework overview. (a) Decentralised inference: each agent’s frozen VLA backbone (Octo-Base or π0.5) encodes its local observation. Its CoLA module compresses the backbone feature into a compact message (dm = 64), decodes the partner’s message, and concatenates the result with its own representation to form zi. This vector conditions a U-Net action head via FiLM, which predicts a coordinated action chunk (K = 10). (b) Adapter and action-head training: backbone features are cached offline and the backbones stay frozen. Only the CoLA modules are trained with a behavioural cloning loss, with gradients flowing end-to-end through the communication channel. (c) Multi-agent broadcast: each agent broadcasts its message to all other agents and receives theirs, so the same design scales to N ≥ 3 agents.

papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
authors: Xinnan Dai, Kaiqi Yang, Yaxin Li, Cheng Luo, Wanli Li, Mingqing Xiao, Xinyang Jiang, Daoan Zhang, Kaitao Song, Fengze Liu, Zefan Cai, Caihua Shan
bullets: Addresses the gap between static language benchmarks and real-world embodied action.

Provides a foundation for evaluating LLMs as agents connecting language, tools, and the physical world.

papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.
Combines two policies’ score or velocity fields during sampling to control exploration–exploitation trade-offs.
Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Satoshi Yamamori, Jun Morimoto
bullets: Existing TTC improves execution by selecting among candidates but requires recomputing this selection at every execution because the policy remains frozen.

The framework uses a fixed verifier to score flow-matching VLA candidates, executes their weighted aggregate, and distills successful episodes into LoRA parameters using the standard flow-matching loss.
It requires no additional reinforcement learning or teacher-generation rollouts, reusing supervision produced during TTC.
On 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling from 10 episodes per task raises verifier-free single-candidate success from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of eight-candidate aggregation’s improvement.
Applying aggregation after distillation further increases success from 76.4% to 82.3%, with gains also observed on LIBERO-Long and distribution-shifted LIBERO-plus.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the conflict between vision/proprioception before contact and force sensing during contact.
Uses separate experts: a base vision-dominated expert for non-contact behavior and a force-aware expert for contact stages.
Applies a contact-localized curriculum that progressively restores vision and masks state tokens to reduce shortcut learning.
Real-robot tests cover pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping.
Reports 20–40 percentage-point overall success gains over the strongest baseline on each task, while retaining non-contact performance and robustness to held-out grasp heights.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of DEFT-VLA. A shared VLM conditions a task-adapted base expert for non-contact behavior and a force-specialized contact expert for critical contact stages. The contact expert is initialized from the base expert and receives an additional force token. During contact-expert post-training, the contact-localized curriculum gradually restores image clarity and the original state tokens to suppress visual and proprioceptive shortcuts. At inference, a lightweight stage estimator fuses task-conditioned visual features, robot state, and causal wrench history, while a contact-stage router selects the active expert. Snowflake and flame symbols denote frozen and trainable modules, respectively.

In each row, the first three frames show the vision-dominated preparatory stage handled by the task-adapted base expert, while the last three show the critical contact stage handled by the force-specialized contact expert. The central boundary denotes the transition from the base expert to the contact expert.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
authors: Guantian Zheng, Lidong Yu, Tianyu Gao, Jiaxing Chen, Jiashu Li, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the lack of inference-time control over acceleration, braking, and following-distance preferences in end-to-end driving policies.
Distills each teacher’s behavior into a task vector that can be scaled or combined without retraining the planner backbone.
Uses a flow-matching decoder to generate multimodal, kinematically feasible trajectory alternatives.
Introduces Style Alignment Score (SAS) for evaluating human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating.
On NAVSIM navtest, assertiveness changes monotonically across six personas while PDMS stays above 0.90, reaching 0.954; evaluated discrete style labels add limited explanatory power.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.
authors: Jiaxin Fang, Ruitong Liu, Zeyu Lai, Xingyu Wang, Mingyuan Jia, Pingyue Sheng, Weikang Wan, Mengdi Xu, Yuxiang Gao
bullets: Replaces dense layer-wise video–action coupling with 32 Latent Bridge Queries that aggregate visual, language, and proprioceptive information.
Joint video–action supervision adapts visual representations for action prediction, while cross-attention retrieves task-relevant features.
Decouples expert depths and reuses bridge queries, enabling a deep 30-layer Video Expert with an ultralight two-layer Action Expert.
Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the BridgeWAM architecture. Unlike MoT’s matched-depth coupling, BoE decouples expert depths, enabling BRIDGEWAM to use only two layers in the Action DiT while retaining the full Video Expert for learning rich representations of visual information.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang

Simulation and real-robot experiments cover connector insertion, bimanual mating, and screw tightening.
Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.

papers.abstract: In this work, we aim to develop an embodied MLLM agent that understands and solves embodied tasks by learning, abstracting, and reusing transferrable and generalizable behavioral patterns. To this end, we propose StateSkill, a new skill representation for embodied agents, which introduces the concept of "finite-state machines" into skill modeling for effective and efficient skill construction and learning. The core idea of StateSkill is to model embodied interaction experiences as a finite-state machine, where a skill is organized around a set of task-progress states, state transitions, and state-conditioned guidance, enabling embodied agents to dynamically adjust their skills as the task progresses while keeping skill contexts compact and stage-relevant. We further develop StateSkill-Evolve, an experience-driven evolution mechanism that iteratively refines StateSkill through retrospective analysis of new successful and failed state-guided trajectories. Upon this, we introduce StateGRPO, which integrates StateSkill evolution and model optimization via state-conditioned GRPO into a unified iterative learning loop, enabling state-conditioned skills and model capabilities to co-evolve and reinforce each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods and trained model (i.e., StateSkill-Agent) across various embodied tasks.
authors: Changxu Wei, Jingyi Zhang, Zhiyu Zheng, Tianyi Lin, Yixian Zhang, Yunpeng Qing, Jingyuan Liu, Zhi Hou, Jiaxing Huang
bullets: Motivation: Embodied agents need transferable, generalizable behavioral patterns while keeping skill context efficient.
StateSkill represents skills with task-progress states, transitions, and state-conditioned guidance for dynamic, stage-relevant behavior.
StateSkill-Evolve refines skills by retrospectively analyzing successful and failed state-guided trajectories.
StateGRPO combines skill evolution with state-conditioned policy optimization in an iterative co-evolution loop.
Experiments report effectiveness across various embodied tasks, though specific results and scope details are not provided.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. (b) StateSkill abstracts shared behavioral patterns from embodied trajectories into a finitestate machine, equipping each task-progress state with language guidance, a transition gate, and trajectory-derived action priors. (c) StateSkill-Evolve iteratively refines StateSkill by reviewing new successful and failed state-guided trajectories and validating candidate revisions. (d) StateGRPO integrates StateSkill evolution and state-conditioned embodied agent optimization into a unified iterative loop, enabling StateSkill and model capabilities to co-evolve.

Figure 1: Motivation. (a) Imitating from task-specific demonstrations offers limited transferability and generalization. (b) Textual LLM skills face two key challenges for embodied agents: Limited Skill Representation in representing complex behavioral experiences in interactive physical environments; and Limited Skill Efficiency due to loading entire skill descriptions that introduce redundant and irrelevant context. (c) StateSkill organizes shared behavioral patterns into finite-state machines as skills and dynamically provides state-conditioned guidance as tasks progress, while new interaction experiences enable StateSkill and the model to co-evolve and mutually reinforce each other.

papers.abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Haitao Shen, Guanlin Li, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Problem: Fine-tuned VLA flow-matching policies contract around dominant demonstrated actions, producing redundant test-time candidates.
Method: Sample additional policy trajectories, weight them by flow support estimated with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and apply a detached finite-set KL correction.
Contribution: A training-time proposal-diversification method that increases candidate spread while avoiding the success degradation of Gaussian perturbations.
Results: Oracle best-of-8 RoboCasa success rises from 57.6% to 63.0%; fixed verifiers improve by 2.4–4.9 points in simulation and TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on physical-robot tasks.
Scope: ADS increases training cost, while deployment cost remains unchanged.

papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q-DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine-tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high-failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self-imitation fine-tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q-DEG improves robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine-tuned using data collected from two red-teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q-DEG facilitates sim-to-real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd-env.github.io/qdeg/.
authors: Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita
bullets: VLAs can fail under small shifts in object placement, lighting, textures, and camera pose despite strong in-distribution performance.
