Experiments across three VLA models in simulation show improved robustness in OOD adversarial environments over base models and two red-teaming baselines.
Greater robustness from Q-DEG also supports sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
authors: Yilin Wu, Rutav Shah, Shuaiyi Huang, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Andrea Bajcsy, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses shortcut learning and deployment latency caused by conditioning on all past observations.
Compresses observations, actions, and proprioception into incrementally updated latent memory for VLA policies.
Uses two-stage training: reconstruct past information and estimate task progress, then jointly fine-tune for action prediction.
Improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26% across simulation and real-world tasks.
Reports the lowest inference latency among evaluated memory-augmented VLAs; ablations support using diverse streams without history curation.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to $\pi_{0.5}$ upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure $\pi_{0.5}$. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $\pi_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.
authors: Jianli Sun, Chengxiang Li, Yonglin Tian
bullets: Targets the latency and token overhead caused by frequent external model queries.
CALL reuses standard π0.5 features to predict when assistance is necessary and runs locally.
Astra intervenes during critical recovery events, then returns control to π0.5 after stabilization.
Across 40 LIBERO tasks and 200 episodes, the system achieves 97.5% success versus 95.5% for pure π0.5.
Astra controls only 5.49% of environment steps in the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, using about 5,027 tokens per test episode.

papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
authors: Lonnie Tankersley, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Soroush Korivand
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible language-generated plans and physically feasible robot execution.
An API-hosted LLM produces symbolic task information, while a local Qwen3-VL verifier resolves ambiguous objects and container surrogates.
Deterministic modules handle scene grounding, reachability, collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasping, release verification, and visual assessment.
The system uses symbolic execution feedback for replanning without allowing the LLM or VLM to generate robot motions or coordinates.
Evaluated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim with a simulated Franka Research 3 across pickup, occlusion, keepout, relational placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.

These inputs are fused into a SceneMemory entry containing semantic, geometric, and accessibility attributes, which is then used by the deterministic grounder for object selection and keepout-aware grounding.

papers.abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.
authors: Edward Sun, Christopher Leet, Sravanthi Machcha, Achyutha Menon, Tzu Kit Chan, Yuchen Cui, Jay Chooi
bullets: Introduces RoboHarm, a benchmark for harmful robot instructions across text, code, vision, and robot-control interfaces.
Tests seven frontier models in MuJoCo simulations and on a physical bimanual robot while holding models fixed and varying only the interface.
Refusal rates drop sharply from 73% for text requests to 18–25% with robot control in simulation; physical-robot results are similarly low.
Transcripts suggest failures arise from missed hazards, failure to infer consequences, or acting despite recognizing harm.
Refusals often depend on uncertainty about object identity rather than the harmfulness of the action itself.

papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation will be released as open source.
authors: Bince Qu, Wei Chen, Bo Zhang
bullets: Targets generalist embodied manipulation without directly training a vision-language-action model.
Provides LLM agents with a visual-geometric control panel for understanding and invoking robot tasks.
Uses Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the RoboHarness interface.
Reports better performance than state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks.
The implementation is planned for open-source release.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for robots because they generalize across diverse environments. However, this requires their safety alignment to also hold in unseen environments. Existing red-teaming assumes an adversary who optimizes the prompt, the pixels, or text in the environment, and existing benchmarks ask whether a planner recognizes or mitigates a hazard in a fixed scene. Neither asks whether a refusal the planner has already given survives an ordinary change to the environment. We ask that question by placing a single everyday object into the environment, with no pixel, gradient, or prompt under adversarial control. On $846$ tasks that a constitution-guarded planner initially refuses, we find $20.2\%$ of tasks can be flipped to compliance by one or more objects, and the number of objects differs from one task to another. In addition, the object need not be chosen for the task, i.e., items drawn from a fixed list, with no knowledge of the environment or the instruction, bypass safety about as often as items proposed for the specific task. We qualitatively contrast the tasks bypassed most and least often and find that the distinction lies in how conspicuous the hazard is in the instruction and environment. Susceptibility to safety bypass is therefore a property of the task, which we call its \emph{malleability}, and we show that it can be predicted before the target is ever queried. A composite of signals read from a small open-source VLM identifies malleable tasks $2.4\times$ as often as picking at random. Everyday objects, whether placed by an adversary or introduced by ordinary rearrangement of the environment, are thus sufficient to overturn a refusal. Because susceptibility is determined by how a task is specified, we recommend assessing malleability per task prior to deployment.
bullets: Among 846 initially refused tasks, 20.2% were flipped to compliance by adding one or more objects.
Objects selected without knowing the task or environment bypassed safety about as often as task-specific objects.
Malleability varies by task and is linked qualitatively to how conspicuously the hazard is specified.
Signals from a small open-source VLM identified malleable tasks 2.4× more often than random selection.
The authors recommend assessing refusal malleability for each task before deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the malleability of safety refusals in embodied VLM planners, introducing a novel concept for assessing safety alignment in unseen environments.
papers.title: Refusals That Bend: Measuring and Predicting Task Malleability in Embodied VLM Planners
papers.tldr: A single ordinary object can overturn an embodied VLM planner’s safety refusal, and task-specific malleability can be predicted before deployment.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have made them capable generalist physical agents for a range of manipulation tasks. However, successful operation in an unfamiliar environment may require an agent to seek task-relevant information through interaction when it is absent from the observations: it may need to determine where a relevant object is, inspect an unobserved property, or discover the effect of an unfamiliar tool. We thus introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively acquire task-relevant information through physical interaction, use the resulting evidence to adapt subsequent actions, and autonomously decide when to commit to task completion. RoboQuest comprises ten mobile manipulation tasks centered on three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. We evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, as well as a $π_{0.5}$ policy fine-tuned on the full-episode demonstrations we release. The best agent succeeds in only 23\% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds. Isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks are built from, with the hidden information supplied, show that the agents can carry out most of the required actions, and our failure analysis attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. Our failure analysis further finds that the agents often stop exploring too early as they make decisions before observing the required evidence for task completion. We also find that agents rarely prevent or repair the disturbances caused by their exploration. Moreover, learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models.
bullets: Introduces ten mobile-manipulation tasks spanning search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing.
Agents must acquire task-relevant evidence, adapt actions, and decide when to complete a task.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task $π_{0.5}$ policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.
bullets: Existing VLA action representations mainly model trajectories without explicitly capturing the visual dynamics actions induce.
ViDAL trains an Action VAE to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent space with future scene dynamics.
The resulting plug-in action interface is compatible with multiple VLA architectures and can optionally support future-video prediction.
ViDAL achieves 98.1% average success on LIBERO and improves π₀.₅ on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and 33.2% to 43.1% (Random).
It also reports absolute success-rate gains on real-world Franka and ARX robot platforms, though the abstract does not specify the baseline setup or broader limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark-agnostic framework for evaluating behavioural robustness in tabletop manipulation.
Extends LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across four task suites, seven perturbation conditions, and three VLA models.
Analyses motion smoothness, efficiency, gripper behaviour, and variability in successful trajectories.
Finds that perturbations can substantially change successful behaviour even when task success rates remain comparable.
Argues that behavioural metrics should complement task success rate for more complete robustness assessment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, but their zero-shot generalization in new tasks and environments remains limited, and their reliance on specialized training keeps them from benefiting directly from rapidly advancing general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs). In parallel, recent agentic robotic systems leverage VLMs for high-level reasoning or coding agents for robot control, but often depend on extensive external models and tools, introducing additional complexity and cost. This motivates us to ask: Can a general-purpose VLM itself operate a robot more like the human teleoperator by reasoning directly from observations, issuing actions, and continuously adapting to execution feedback, without relying on external models such as learned action experts, coding agents or grounding tools like SAM3? In this work, we introduce MotorMind, a robot manipulation harness that connects VLM-proposed mid-level actions to deterministic robot control and feedback, with asynchronous monitoring and background memory updates. Without task-specific policy training, coding agents, or additional grounding tools such as SAM3, MotorMind achieves 66.7% success on the base LIBERO-PRO suites and 53.8% under perturbations, compared with at most 13.3% and 19.2%, respectively, for the prior zero-shot methods we evaluate. The same interface reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 robot across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings. Replacing the backbone with a stronger VLM further improves performance, while the remaining failures - primarily due to visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge - decrease as VLM capability improves. These results show that a general-purpose VLM, when equipped with an appropriate mid-level action representation and asynchronous execution harness, can perform effective zero-shot robotic manipulation.
bullets: Targets limited zero-shot generalization and the complexity of systems requiring specialized policies, coding agents, or grounding tools.
Uses a robot manipulation harness with VLM-proposed mid-level actions, deterministic control, asynchronous monitoring, and background memory updates.
Achieves 66.7% success on base LIBERO-PRO and 53.8% under perturbations, versus at most 13.3% and 19.2% for evaluated prior zero-shot methods.
Reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings.
Performance improves with stronger VLMs; remaining failures mainly involve visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge.

papers.abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user's objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.
authors: Xiaomeng Ye, Krishna Jaganathan, Gyubeum Lim, Gunjan Chhablani, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Zsolt Kira
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying generalist manipulation policies in new homes or offices, where unadapted pickup success can be ineffective and real-data collection is costly.

Uses a privileged simulation oracle to produce demonstrations, followed by two-stage fine-tuning on public assets and the user’s objects.
Across 101 scanned campus environments, the pipeline generated over 68,000 pickup demonstrations from 852 receptacles.
The personalized policy achieved 62.5% simulated target-scene success and 63.9% success on a real Stretch 3 evaluation subset, versus 66.7% simulated success on those tasks.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes.
authors: Junjie Lu, Chuheng Zhang, Yucen Wang, Yuhua Jiang, Xinyao Qin, Min Xu, Li Zhao
bullets: Addresses VLA adaptation under limited robot interaction, computation, and safety constraints.
Learns a context-conditioned noise distribution as an adaptation interface for flow-matching-based VLAs.
Implements the interface with PPO, SAC, and AWR, while providing an information-theoretic analysis.
Evaluates variants on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks across multiple resource constraints.
Offers practical guidance for selecting NSL variants under different training and deployment regimes.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.

papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting robot interaction data and the lack of action labels in human videos.
Learns continuous latent actions from frame transitions using perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals.
Pre-trains a vision-language-action policy, aligns it to the target robot embodiment, and applies task-specific post-training.
Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, it improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% when annotated human video increases from 1K to 5K hours.
The resulting policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

papers.tldr: LAPT-Scale uses continuous latent actions learned from large-scale human videos to pre-train generalist robot policies, substantially improving real-robot performance as video data scales.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
authors: Faith Ogunwoye, Didar Seyidov, Konstantin Gubernatorov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: VLA commands arrive sparsely and irregularly, potentially causing abrupt motion near people.
The benchmark isolates controller effects by replaying the same commands and arrival traces across alternatives.
Interpolation reduced modeled p99 jerk by 83% on delayed human-motion traces, with a 2.0 cm tracking cost; jerk-limited generation reduced jerk further at greater cost.
Results across three VLA pipelines showed inconsistent links between entropy discontinuities and motion quality, and entropy gating helped only one pipeline.
On a physical UR3, interpolation reduced accelerometer-derived jerk in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not show the same contrast.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
authors: Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
bullets: Addresses representation drift and weakened out-of-distribution generalization when adapting pre-trained robot policies with few demonstrations.
Uses a two-stage process: retrieve similar pre-training features and align target representations, then fine-tune while constraining changes to retrieved representations.
Evaluated with Diffusion Policy and GR00T across 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot.
Improves average fine-tuning success by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, outperforming compared baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RARA. (Left) A policy is first pre-trained on diverse robot data. (Middle) To adapt it to a target task, RARA first retrieves pre-training demonstrations of a similar skill, such as removing a lid from a flask for the target task of opening a blender lid. It then aligns the target representation with their pre-trained representation, which it keeps as an anchor during fine-tuning. (Right) Across 13 simulated and real-world tasks, RARA improves the average ID and OOD success over fine-tuning by 11.6 points.

Figure 4: ID (top) and OOD (bottom) scenes for one RoboTwin, one RoboCasa and one real-robot task. Baselines. We compare RARA with five baselines. They cover the two common ways to reuse pre-training knowledge during fine-tuning: training on pre-training data (Co-FT and STRAP) and keeping the policy close to the pre-trained one (RETAIN and BlindVLA). FT fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations only. Co-FT also trains on the retrieved pre-training demonstrations Dret (§4.1) with the behavior-cloning loss. STRAP (Memmel et al., 2025) instead retrieves pre-training sub-trajectories that match the target demonstrations under dynamic time warping, and co-trains on them. RETAIN (Yadav et al., 2026) merges the weights of the pre-trained and fine-tuned policies. BlindVLA (Kachaev et al., 2026) aligns the policy’s visual representations with those of a frozen pre-trained visual encoder during fine-tuning. See Appx. D.2 for details.

Figure 5: Real-robot results (success rate, %, mean± std over three runs) with GR00T N1.7 pretrained on DROID. RARA outperforms baselines in all target tasks, ID and OOD settings.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses robust fine-tuning of VLA robot policies for manipulation via representation alignment; fits robot learning and VLA topics.
papers.title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: RARA improves few-shot robotic policy adaptation by aligning target demonstrations with retrieved pre-training representations and preserving those representations during fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $\tau=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Abdelwahed Khamis, Mohammad Ali Armin, Lars Petersson
bullets: Motivation: alarms can be too late to enable recovery, or can disrupt executions that would have succeeded.
Method: restore simulator and policy states at checkpoints, compare counterfactual interventions, and find the latest recoverable checkpoint.
Contribution: a framework for measuring recoverability and intervention cost jointly with monitor performance.
Findings: recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair; favourable detection scores do not necessarily reduce intervention cost.
Scope/limitation: under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, ideal detectors tolerate only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before resets become counterproductive.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Measuring recoverability and its dependence on intervention. Left: Counterfactual restarts from saved checkpoints of a failed OpenVLAOFT/LIBERO-Plus execution yield observed success rates (teal) and lower-quantile recoverability estimates (purple). At τ = 0.5, step 48 is the last recoverable checkpoint, while step 56 no longer satisfies the recovery criterion. Right: Median recoverability horizons (circles), interquartile ranges (bars), and median runtime-monitor alarm times (black symbols) across policy settings. Continue and escalate denote CONTINUE and scripted RECOVER; ticks show median horizons at τ = 0.3 and τ = 0.7. On OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus, 14/66 failures contain a qualifying checkpoint under CONTINUE, 33/66 under RECOVER, and 34/66 under their union.

Fig. 3. Monitor alarms often arrive after the recoverability horizon. Across four policy settings, left: fraction of alarmed failures whose alarm occurs after the horizon, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals; right: alarm-minus-horizon lag, with medians and interquartile ranges. Positive lag indicates late detection. Results include failures for which both an alarm and a recoverability horizon are defined under the corresponding intervention. Purple denotes CONTINUE; amber denotes scripted RECOVER, labelled “escalate” in the figure.

TABLE I: Break-even stop-and-reset worksheet. Inputs to Eq. (9) for steps-since-progress at its validation-selected nominal 5% false-alarm operating point. T̄s,FA is the mean natural duration of the successful episodes that are actually false-alarmed. The realised false-alarm rate f substantially exceeds the break-even rate f ∗ on both primary cells.

papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual evaluation of VLA runtime monitors for robot policy recovery; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
papers.tldr: RESCUE evaluates robot runtime alarms by whether acting on them actually improves task outcomes, not merely by detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA, which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.
authors: Yuechen Luo, He Chong, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu, Hexin Zhang, Ruiqi Zhang, Ziying Song, Lei Yang, Zhi-Xin Yang, Fuxi Wen
bullets: Scalar trajectory rewards provide limited, non-actionable feedback for specific planning errors, especially in long-tail scenarios.
Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation uses driving scores to route student rollouts, distilling token-level corrections for risky trajectories and self-imitation for reliable ones.
A progressively built teacher supplies corrective guidance through knowledge pretraining, planning/refinement supervised fine-tuning, and self-refinement rejection sampling.
At inference, the model plans in a single pass without explicit reflection or iterative refinement.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive show competitive planning performance and over 90% lower training time than RL.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Reflect-VLA. Reflective Guidance is constructed from trajectory evaluation and used as privileged information to train a refinement-capable teacher. Dual-OPSD then transfers corrective distributions to the student on risky trajectories while preserving reliable student trajectories. Only the student is used for single-pass inference.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons and token-level analysis. Left and middle: trajectories generated by the unguided student, guidance-conditioned teacher, and distilled student. Right: distributions over special trajectory tokens at critical decoding steps under the same student-generated prefix. Each token encodes a relative displacement quantized at 0.01 m resolution; e.g., <|x_208|> represents a 2.08 m forward displacement for the next waypoint.

Figure 1: From Reflective Guidance to Internalized Planning. (a) Reflective Guidance corrects an unsafe initial trajectory during iterative inference, revealing substantial planning gains. (b) Reflect-VLA transfers these gains through Dual-OPSD by aligning teacher and student token distributions along student-generated trajectories. (c) Across different model scales, Reflect-VLA improves planning performance over SFT while requiring substantially less training time than RL, enabling guidance-free single-pass planning.

papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
authors: Yang Wang, Ping Liu, Ruiyu Wang, Xuhua Chen, Lingfeng Zhang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks where execution state must be tracked and previously visible evidence recovered.
Uses a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet temporal compressor with progress prediction and action-conditioned reconstruction.
Adds a task-conditioned frame retriever and encodes selected frames with 16 spatial tokens; the compressor is frozen during joint retrieval-policy training.
On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.
Cup-swap failures indicate persistent object-identity tracking remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
authors: Min Lin, Bokai Zhou, Jianqi Lin, Kaiyuan Yang, Yicheng Chang, Junjie Yu, Xiaofan Liu, Jianhua Han, Rui Li, Shen Zhao, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets future-grounded Effect tokens rather than actions alone.
Builds temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrations, robot responses, and sparse visual transitions.
Uses flow matching to predict Effects, then a state-conditioned decoder generates action chunks.
Supports shared Effect modeling across single- and dual-arm embodiments.
On DexJoCo, achieves 50.97% overall success and leads on all five bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
authors: Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit future-state supervision in VLAs and the inference cost and error propagation of WAMs.
Uses an action-to-future paradigm: predicted futures condition on action features, not vice versa.
End-to-end training lets future-state prediction supervise the policy without allowing prediction errors to affect actions.
Backbone-agnostic design is instantiated with both vision-language and video-generative backbones.
Demonstrates a 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and up to 13% absolute gains over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our Forward Dynamics Models. The context expert encodes visual observations and the instruction to guide the action expert. During training, the generation expert predicts future states from context and action features; its loss backpropagates through these action features to complement action imitation. This asymmetric connection lets future supervision shape the policy while keeping action prediction independent of predicted futures. At inference, the action expert generates actions using the required context features, skipping future generation.

During training, action imitation and future prediction are jointly optimized; the future loss backpropagates through action features to supervise the policy. At inference, FDM denoises action chunks using only the current observation and instruction, skipping the future-generation branch marked as training only while retaining context processing.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
authors: Gangyi Li, LuYao Wang, Jingfu Sun, Jingyi Yuan, Hang Liu, Hao Zong, Yujia Hu, Tingting Gao, Jianyong Wang, Xu Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting multimodal observations and changing user goals into executable actions under product constraints.
Builds closed-loop interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, validated by execution outcomes and semantic criteria.
Uses staged learning—supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and reinforcement learning with DPER token-level evidence routing.
Combines generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency for training rewards.

Scores 77.44 on BFCL v4 and leads reported metrics on JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, while results on other public benchmarks are mixed; quadruped case studies demonstrate search, replanning, and failure reporting.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
authors: Zile Zhong, Yuxin Du, Tao Lin, Haoxiao Wang, Wei Dai, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that action supervision does not explicitly teach VLAs to anticipate scene evolution.
Uses optical-flow-based future motion prediction to focus representations on task-relevant motion rather than static appearance.
Preserves predictive representations during policy learning by regulating representation diversity and decoupling representation learning from action optimization.
Achieves a 91.1% tier-averaged success rate on Meta-World MT50, a 13.0% relative gain over a non-predictive baseline.
Shows stronger performance than evaluated baselines on real-world single-arm and bimanual AgileX tasks with 0.87B parameters, lower GPU memory use, and higher inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
authors: Xule Gao, Xi Wang, Zehua Zang, Rui Wang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun
bullets: Problem: Step-wise imitation can overfit to demonstration paths and offers limited guidance after execution deviates from them.
Method: Relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and uses goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize key-state reachability.
Contribution: Shifts VLA post-training from trajectory imitation toward recoverable, goal-directed behavior from feasible off-demonstration states.
Results: Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning on LIBERO and MetaWorld, with stronger robustness under shifts and perturbations on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-ReAct.

papers.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
authors: Weiwei Chen, Chenghao Xu, Meiling Yu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Long-tailed demonstration data can cause shared policies to favor action patterns from data-rich head tasks, harming under-represented tail tasks.
The method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence from instruction- and action-related signals, then removes it to create counterfactual observations.
Counterfactual predictions reinforce links among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with supervision adjusted by task demonstration frequency.
It requires no additional data or region-level annotations and adds no deployment-time computation.
Experiments across simulated benchmarks, multiple VLA architectures, and real robots show improved tail-task learning while maintaining head-task performance.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM's native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM's perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
authors: Jingkun Yi, Shujie Zhang, Zirui Zhou, Haoxiao Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yuhang Dong, Xudong Xu, Xing Shen, Tao Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing pretrained VLM reasoning capabilities through a unified continuous-action interface.
Projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera view, making action semantics visible in the VLM’s perceptual context.
Represents robot actions through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, avoiding robot-action pretraining and extra action modules.
Supports both zero-shot manipulation and trajectory-based fine-tuning in the same continuous action space.
Enables generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, as described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis
bullets: Targets long-horizon manipulation, where robots must retain useful history while retracting unsupported conclusions.
Uses a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor, without policy retraining.
Links derived relations and completed conditions to supporting facts, then withdraws affected conclusions when evidence changes.
Schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries after disturbances.
Across 51 physical trials, mean recorded progress improved from 57% to 91% for intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% for sequence recall.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.
authors: Justin Tien-Smith, Matthew Pidden, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Introduces a real-robot benchmark spanning six tabletop spatial tasks: object state, relative size, referential description, relational placement, ordinal position, and counting.
Compares in-distribution and out-of-distribution spatial configurations while controlling for object and motor unfamiliarity.
Adds diagnostics for physical execution, wording sensitivity, object-task associations, and recognizing when no action is needed.
Evaluates 4,092 episodes on the SO-101 robot arm, including demonstrations and rollouts from five VLA policies.

Across three fully evaluated policies, success drops from 67.5–73.3% on in-distribution configurations to 40.7–52.0% on out-of-distribution configurations; direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
authors: Jaewoo Lee, Jeongyeon Seo, Sihyun Cho, Gyeongrak Choe, Yutong Wang, Bavin Saravanan, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi, H. Jin Kim, Seungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee
bullets: Aerial manipulation suffers from partial observability and fragile physical interactions, making ordinary execution feedback insufficient for program refinement.
The proposed View-and-Probe framework generates diagnostic programs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes or test likely failure causes through targeted interactions.
Across six simulated tasks, false completion declarations fell from 25 to 5, while final success increased from 31.7% to 75% under the same agent configuration and task limit.
Programs refined with Active Feedback in simulation transferred to a physical aerial manipulator without source-code changes and completed multi-stage tasks.
The approach is demonstrated within the scope of simulated evaluation and selected real-world aerial manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Fly-by-Code. Bottom: The program refinement loop. The coding agent translates a task prompt into an executable task program using shared robot APIs. Following execution, it enters the Active Feedback (AF) stage to acquire diagnostic evidence, iteratively refining the program until it decides to terminate the revision process. Top: During AF, the agent synthesizes a diagnostic program to resolve execution uncertainties. View actively navigates to informative viewpoints (e.g., inspecting a basket from above to verify placement). Probe conducts diagnostic physical tests (e.g., testing door articulation with an arc motion after a straight pull fails).

The diagnostic program acquired views of the destinations and nearby floor, which place both tools near floor level, and the agent rejected the reported success. The next task program converts the measurements into a push-response model for contact selection. papers.abstract: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
bullets: Targets the lack of consistent benchmarks for tactile-enabled manipulation across simulation and reality.
Organizes contact-rich tasks into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions with paired sim-real settings.
Evaluates VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies, including different tactile representations and integration strategies.
Introduces OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework based on the best-performing design choices.
Uses the paired benchmark to study sim-real co-training and factors influencing cross-domain policy learning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically operate on RGB images produced by a fixed camera image signal processor (ISP), leaving the imaging pipeline outside the learning and evaluation loop. We systematically examine the consequences of this overlooked design choice across five fundamental ISP dimensions: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth. Our analysis reveals that RAW-to-RGB processing materially shapes both action prediction and manipulation success, with different ISP dimensions exerting substantially different effects. Guided by these findings, we introduce RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies while concentrating its capacity on the imaging factors relevant to embodied behavior. We further present RawVLA-Bench, a RAW-domain manipulation benchmark to expose image processing as an explicit evaluation variable across clean and adverse acquisition conditions. Experiments on RawVLA-Bench show that RawVLA preserves performance under standard conditions while substantially improving robustness under degraded imaging, establishing adaptive RAW processing as an effective interface between physical cameras and embodied policies.
bullets: Fixed RGB camera pipelines can significantly affect action prediction and manipulation success.
The study evaluates five ISP factors: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth.
RawVLA is a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies.
RawVLA-Bench evaluates RAW-domain manipulation under clean and adverse acquisition conditions.
Experiments show improved robustness to degraded imaging without sacrificing standard-condition performance.

papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) has become a standard lens for measuring and intervening on semantic information through the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). A growing body of work has begun extending this perspective to vision-language-action (VLA) models, but the dynamical nature of embodied interaction introduces an additional challenge. Unlike semantic attributes commonly studied in LLMs, such as gender or language, a physical quantity of interest (QoI) in a VLA evolves jointly with the system dynamics: the representation influences the actions selected by the policy, which alter the physical state and, in turn, the next representation. In this paper, we develop a theoretical, signature-based formulation of the LRH for VLA that unifies representations and policies. On the representation side, we establish the existence of representations from which the future evolution of a QoI under a candidate action trajectory can be recovered via linear probing. On the policy side, we introduce a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks. This structure yields a monotonic change in the expected future QoI along linear paths in natural parameter space, enabling linear steering. We first validate this structure in a controlled oracle setting, then examine whether the same probing and steering mechanisms emerge in a pretrained VLA.
bullets: Addresses the challenge that physical quantities in embodied systems evolve through feedback between representations, actions, and environment dynamics.
Develops a signature-based theoretical formulation unifying VLA representations and policies.
Shows that future quantity evolution under candidate action trajectories can be recovered through linear probing.
Introduces a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks, enabling linear steering along natural-parameter paths.
Validates the framework in a controlled oracle setting and investigates its emergence in a pretrained VLA.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Linear probing and steering in VLA representations. Given a current state x with representation λ(x), candidate action trajectories uj define action-conditioned linear probes that predict the propagated quantity of interest (QoI), ψ(Fuj (x)) = ⟨λ(x), γψ(uj)⟩. Steering the representation along λψ(x), via λ(x) 7→ λ(x) + αλψ(x), monotonically shifts the propagated QoI, allowing the policy to favor lower or higher physical outcomes.

Figure 3: Closed-loop concept steering. Natural-language labels “Approach mugj” are used only to describe the corresponding concepts, not as additional policy instructions ℓ 7→ ℓ′. End-effector trajectories over six re-planned chunks (2.4 s) in a held-out episode, starting from the same state (×), with αDϕ⊤λψ applied at each re-plan. The QoI is ψ(x) = −d(EE,mugj), targeting (a) the white mug (j = 1) and (b) the yellow-and-white mug (j = 2). Positive and negative α encourage and suppress approach, respectively. In both cases the policy still heads for the white mug, its first subgoal; steering biases the path and pace towards or away from the targeted mug without changing the object the policy goes to.

The probe direction without the Jacobian, γψ (blue), has the right sign but a smaller and QoI-dependent effect. The static-probe direction (black) decreases the three heights and the negative distance of the white mug to its plate, i.e. it steers the wrong way. The task-level QoIs are negative distances, so an increase means moving towards the goal.
